speechtext:
Mr. F. B. CARVELL (Carleton, N.B.) asked for leave to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the desirability, in the public interest, of immediately enlarging the power of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the contracts regarding fuses, etc., called the Meredith-Duff Commission, by providing for widening the scope of the inquiry into the matters referred to the commission.
And leave having been granted,
He said: I wish to present to the House certain facts as the result of the investigation of the Meredith-Duff Commission, so called. In doing so it is not my intention to in any way refer to any evidence given before the commission as indicating what has been proven or has not been proven, or anything of that kind. I realize that this is a matter which is really sub judice at the present time, and a matter to be desired by the commission, and that it would be highly improper on my part, especially as I am a counsel before the commissioners, to make any comment or reflection of any kind. Therefore, in the remarks I make, I will endeavour to confine my statements and my arguments entirely to the question of whether or not it is in the public interest to enlarge the scope of the inquiry. And in order to make the discussion as short as possible, I wish to refer to many

things generally, without quoting page and date. It is within the knowledge of every member of this House that some weeks ago the right hon. leader of the Opposition moved that a Committee of this House he appointed for the purpose of investigating matters relating to the Shell Committee, which ceased to exist some time in the latter part of November, 1015. That motion was voted down by the House,	and
two days afterwards the right	hon.
Prime Minister informed the House that the Governor General in Council had appointed a commission for the purpose of investigating three contracts specially mentioned and one other in case it should come within the purview of the commission, or words to that effect. I am not going to read that Order in Council, 'because it is on Hansard and is a matter of record. Since Wednesday of last week that commission has been proceeding under the terms of the Order in Council, witnesses have been sworn and examined and cross-examined. Perhaps it would not be anjiss if I should take this opportunity of stating publicly that I feel that counsel representing the Government is presenting the case in as fair and as able a manner as is possible- and that is saying a great deal when I am discussing Mr. I. F. Hellmuth. But, Sir, the investigation is developing a condition of affairs regarding the doings and status of the old Shell Committee which was certainly a revelation to every person who had anything to do with the commission, and which, I think, must be a revelation to a large majority of the members of this House. I refer to the fact, brought out before the commission, that at least from and after the first day of October, 1914, down to the day when the Shell Committee ceased to exist, on November 30, 1915, four members of that committee, namely Messrs. Bertram, Cantley, Watts and E. Carnegie, legally occupied the position of contractors with the British Government, as represented 'by the Minister of Militia and Defence. All of these gentlemen have not in any way claimed that they were entitled to any part of the profits which may have come out of the transaction. I want that to be particularly stated, 'because three of them have already been examined and have repudiated the idea of taking profits to themselves. But they all contend that legally they would be entitled to the profits if profits were made, and I think the converse would be true-at least, I know that this was admitted by one of them-that if

losses were made they would be responsible for theip. I think they all say that they approached the Prime Minister and brought up the question as to what their position would be in case of losses taking place. The Prime Minister was very careful, they say, not to make any promise; he told them that they would cross that bridge when they came to it. They went on; that bridge was not reached; therefore they were not called upon to discuss it. The substance of it all, however, was this: the Prime Minister said:	"We want the shells; go on,
and if there are losses we will have to discuss that later." That, I think, would be a fair way of putting it; at least, that is the way the witnesses have placed it before the commission.
I shall not go over the correspondence leading up to the first contract, because it was placed on Hansard by the Minister of Militia in an address delivered in this House on the 25th or 26th of January last. However, the sum and substance of it was that a number of cablegrams having passed between the British War Office and the Minister of Militia, we had authority-I say " we;" I mean the Dominion of Canada; I would call that the Government of Canada-had authority to supply the British Government with 100,000 empty shrapnel shells, 18-pounders, at $8.55 each, and 100,000 empty 15-pounder shrapnel shells at $8.30 each. On the first day of October a contract was entered into between the Minister of Militia and Defence, representing the British War Office, and four gentlemen of a committee of seven or eight. I want to read this agreement, as found on page 30 of the evidence taken by the commission :

speechtext: What does it refer to?

It proceeds to deal with the drawing of specifications, contract to be fulfilled according to the specification, and things of that kind. (Reading):
The said shells shall be made of such materials and components and in accordance with the drawings and specifications hereto annexed, and signed by the parties hereto.
The parties of the first part agree to deliver the said shell as follows, viz. 18-pounder mark III shells, delivery to be made to the party of the second part or to his authorized officers f.o.b. Montreal to the order of the party of the second part.
The shells shall be subject to inspection and such tests as may be required by the party of the second part during the process of manufacture, and shall moreover, be subject after manufacture completed to inspection and acceptance at the factory by the party of the second part; the approval and acceptance of any one lot of shells shall not be evidence of approval of acceptance of any other lot.
The prices to be paid for the said shells shall be for 18-pounder shells, $8.55 per shell.
For 15-pounder shells, $8.30 per shell, to be paid within ten days after the date of delivery, subject to certification of the invoices by the authorized officers appointed by the party of the second part.
In witness whereof the parties have hereunto set their hand the day and year first herein written.
The signatories to this document are Alexander Bertram, Thomas Cantley, G. W. Watts,. E. Carnegie, Sam Hughes, Minister of Militia and Defence for Canada; and the document is executed in the presence of D. Carnegie.
A second contract dated October 20, was entered into between the same parties for the supply of a certain number of boxes in which to transport these shells, also some cartridge eases. That will be found on page 33 of the proceedings of the commission. I do not think it is necessary to read it, because the wording is almost exactly the same as the one which I have just read, except, of course, as to the quantities, prices and specifications. Then they immediately entered into negotiations for the third lot, and in order to make myself thoroughly understood I feel that I shall have to read the negotiations with regard to this particular lot. This was for 200,000 18-pounder shrapnel, fixed ammunition, and 400,000 empty shrapnel shells. In this correspondence by cable the War Office was always addressed and signed as "Troopers " and the Militia Department of Canada was addressed as " Militia." This is a cable to " Troopers in London, the War Office, " dated November 24, 1014:
Referring to your cable 2025 A-2 and our cable No. 1811-cipher, can undertake supply 200,000 18-pounder shrapnel shells fixed ammunition including propellants but without
>
fuses and packed in ammunition cases delivered f.o.b. Montreal or Halifax by June first. Prices seventeen dollars and sixty-five cents each including boxes.
Can also supply further four hundred thousand 15 or 18-pounder shrapnel shells empty packed in ammunition boxes same delivery, price nine and a quarter dollars each, including boxes, not including cost of inspection. Can also supply fuses and will name price on receipt of specification and drawings. Early decision necessary as price raw materials advancing rapidly.
Please hasten despatch of specifications, gauges, etc., of 18-pounder cartridge cases and fuses and any other ammunition you may require manufactured in Canada will save time.
The answer to that came back on the 26th day of November, from the War Office to the Militia Department, as follows:
Regret that unless price of 18-pounder ammunition without fuse can be reduced to $15 and that of 18-pounder shells to $6, w? cannot place orders.
That was answered on the 2nd of December, 1914, from the Militia Department to the War Office, as follows:
Number 196 cipher. Referring to your cable 2287 A-2, November 30th and our cipher 191 27th November. My committee are proceeding with order, prices being fifteen and six dollars respectively not including wood boxes. Please cable confirmation.
I do not know that we have any evidence of the confirmation, but it was confirmed in some way, and they started out to make the ammunition. Those documents will be found on pages 32 and 33 of the printed report. A number of orders were given from that down to the first day of July. I shall not weary the House by going into the details; in fact, we did not have many details. But we do know that large numbers of orders were given, and that these orders were given out by the Shell Committee, sub-let as they would call it, to different people in different parts of Canada, and I believe that in some cases, when they could not get the parts in Canada, they went to the United States for them, and with that I am finding no fault. Further, they procured material to make shell boxes and things of that kind.
Finally we come to the third contract, which will be found on page 138 of the printed report. As this is a very important contract, I shall take the liberty of reading it:

You will see by looking this over that it includes the 5,000,000 rounds of ammunition to which would be applied and of which would form a part, the 5,000,000 fuses under investigation by the Commission, under contract with the International Arms and Fuse Company and the American Ammunition Company.
I wish to refer to the examination of Mr. D. Carnegie, who from about the 24th of September, 1914, up to about April, 1915, was an employee of the Shell Committee in an advisory capacity, I think as ordnance adviser, and who some time around the first part of April, was made a member of the Shell Committee, still remaining ordnance adviser. Mr. Carnegie has stated on two or three occasions, although I have not the reference with me, that as they were contractors, it was practically their business what price they paid for any component parts of this fixed ammunition, so long as they did not exceed the prices authorized by the War Office, as in this schedule you will find prices for every different article.
Referring to the particular contracts which are being investigated by the Commission, on page 140, the first would be 4-5 Howitzers, empty, 1,666,666, at $16.50 each. Then you will find the same thing with reference to the 18-pounder high explosive, 1,666,666 at $16.50, and the 18-pounder fixed ammunition, that would be shrapnel, 1,666,666 at $18 each. Now, their contention, was that, so long as the component parts all put together did not exceed the prices mentioned in this schedule or authorized by the War Office, it was their business from whom they were purchased, where they purchased, and at what prices, although I do not mean to say that the three gentlemen examined had intimated for a moment that they had any right to retain any of this money for themselves. There again I do not want to discuss the evidence, as I said in opening. But that is the attitude which they have assumed. That attitude was assumed to-day very distinctly by Mr. Cantley and Mr. Watts, f think perhaps more positively by Mr. Watts than the others; but all made the claim that they did not intend to take profits. But they claimed that they had legal right to take profits as long as the total cost of these articles did not exceed the cost authorized by the War Office; that they were within their right, and could act as to that as they had a mind to.
That is the substance of the foundation for the request which I wish to make of
the Government. I have tried to give to the House as accurately as I could, and I only read from the official documents, the position of affairs as it stood up to yesterday morning. Y'esterday morning the cross-examination of Sir Alexander Bertram was commenced by Mr. Johnston, and I am sorry to say it did not get very far along when a very serious question arose as to the powers of the Commission under the reference. But, Mr. Speaker, before I go into that, I have omitted one important thing in the direct examination of Sir Alexander Bertram. It will be found on pages 342 and 343 of the evidence, and as it is very important I wish to read the whole page. This was on the direct examination by Mr. Hellmuth, the Government counsel, and the examination proceeds as follows:
Well, then, General, after that when did you first learn or appreciate the fact that there was going to be some difference, considerable or otherwise, between the War Office prices and the prices at which you had let these contracts to the sub-contractors. When was the earliest that you appreciated that?-A. Oh, it would be probably a week or ten days after. On the first order you mean?
Q. Yes?-A. Yes.
Q. A week or ten days after you appreciated the fact that there was going to be a profit?

 A. Yes, sir. I began to collect prices of the component parts and estimated a surplus in the first place to carry on the business of inspection and the clerical work in connection with the Committee.
Q. Well now was that probably discussed with other members of the committee at first? 

A. No, sir.
Q. Did you discuss it with any one at that time?-A. No, sir, I did not.
Q. When did you first, if at all, discuss that with anyone and with whom?-A. With General Hughes.
Q. And about when was that?-A. Oh, probably November or December.
Q. That is in November or December of 1914?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. And perhaps you will tell me what the discussion was?-A. I came up to Ottawa on some business in connection with the work and showed General Hughes a statement of the profits on the component parts of the shell, which amounted to a considerable sum.
Q. Could you give me any idea of the sum? -A. I have the original. I think on the first 200,000 shells we estimated a surplus of $52,000.
Q. It was quite a sum at all events. Will you continue then? When you told him that, what next?

A. Well, I found that our expenses in running the Shell Committee were a great deal less than I expected, and wondered what we were going to do with the surplus. I think I suggested that if we had a surplus we would turn it over to the Patriotic Fund. General Hughes said: "No, give it back to the War Office."
Hear, hear.
I am certainly trying to give the House the whole story. '
It is much milder than before.
I think I appreciate the position that I occupy to-day, and remarks like that coming from a farmer member of this House are very much out of place.
It is quite true.

I am going to argue this matter as a lawyer, and I am not going to be drawn, away by any farmer backbenchers on the other side of the House. (Reading.)
Q. So that at that time, let me understand it, you were prepared to turn the surplus over to the Patriotic Fund. That is you were not suggesting keeping it?-A. Oh, no.
Q. That had not entered your mind then?- A. No, we were doing it as a patriotic job.
Q. And General Hughes said, "Turn it over to the War Office"?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Now that is in December or November?- A. I couldn't tell. It was some time about November or December. You know at that time we had no idea of getting any future'order.
Q. Then to follow this out for the moment, you did get a number of future orders as you know?-A. Yes.
Q. And was it borne in on your mind when you got these future orders that there were going to be future surpluses?-A. Yes.
Q. What did you do in regard to that, did you communicate that to anybody?-A. No.
Q. Until when? When did you next if at all speak of a possible surplus, and to whom? Carry along from the time you spoke to General Hughes in November or December, whom next did you discuss that with, that there might be a surplus?-A. I would rather not give that for publication, unless the Commission desire it.
Q. You did discuss it did you?-A. Yes, I was asked to report to a high authority on the progress of our work, which I did,
Q. And about what date was that?-A. Some time in May or June. It was after we arrived in Ottawa.
Sir William Meredith:	When he speaks of
high authority perhaps he would not object to say, does he mean Canadian or Imperial?
Mr. Hellmuth:	My learned friend Mr. Johnston tells me that he is quite satisfied.
Q. And in May or June you say it was?

* A. I think some time about the first week in June.
Q. May I ask whether then the amount was still about $52,000 or whether it had grown into millions?-A. No, it had gone up to $14,800,000.
That was in the first week of the inquiry. Then, Sir, I think it was on Monday of this week, a statement was submitted and admitted in evidence, as of date the 30th day of November, 1915, which is the date when the old Shell Committee ceased to exist and the Imperial Munitions Board was created. This will be found on pages 345-6-7 of this report. I do not know that

it will be necessary to incorporate it in Hansard. It takes up every different item or every different contract given by the War Office. It starts in with 100,000 18-pounder shrapnel and 100,000 15-pounder shrapnel, which were included in a contract of the first day of October. It goes on and gives a statement of the value of the material ordered and the balance of the material, or labour-I think they are both called material-in each distinct contract, the total, the War Office prices, and the surpluses or deficits whichever they may be. The sum total of it is that the surplus-that is, the difference between the prices authorized by the War Office and the cost of the articles to the Shell Committee-would be. $41,350,000, or, in other words, legally speaking, the four contractors would have the right to take $41,350,000; but, as they say, morally, they never intended to do it.
Is not that $30,000,000?

I am coming to that in a moment. The statement was $41,360,000, but very -shortly after the document was produced there was an error discovered in it, and that was in reference to the cost of 1,666,666 45-pounder howitzer shells, an error of -somewhere around $11,500,000 That would bring the estimated profit down to the vicinity of $30,000,000 instead of $41,000,000. These matters have not been *checked up, and of course, I do not know whether they are right or wrong; I simply take the document as it was placed before the -Commission.
When Mr. Johnston attempted to crossexamine Sir Alexander Bertram' yesterday morning, he was proceeding along a line that both he and I-I having consulted with him in regard to the matter-believed to be quite proper under the reference. In order that there may be no question as to what took place, I shall read from the record. I do not suppose, Mr. Speaker, that you or the members of the House generally have had an opportunity of seeing this. I went to the gentleman who has charge of the reporting and asked him to get me a number of typewritten copies. He told me that the printed copies would not be ready until late in the afternoon, but I urged him to get me two printed copies if he could do so, and to my surprise, just as the committee adjourned at one o'clock, he brought me two printed copies, but containing only the first hour
MAX' 5, 1916 [DOT]
or hour and a half's evidence. One of these I have given to the Premier, and the other I shall read from myself. I am sorry I was unable to get any more. I am reading from page 371, during Mr. Johnston's cross-examination:
Mr. Ewart: I wish to point out to the Commission that the contracts Mr. Johnston is referring to now are not within the scope of the Commission at all, the boxes, empty shells, and the prices for them.
Witness: I never heard of any $9.25. The four hundred thousand were taken at $6.
Mr. Ewart: I wish to press my objection, that this has nothing to do with the matters in question. If it is followed up it will lead to endless questioning and cross-questioning. If Mr. Johnston goes into these questions we will have to go into other things.
Mr. Johnston: I will read a portion of the letter so that it will call it back to your mind.
On page 32 of the. printed record, in Exhibit No. 28 this appears : " Can also supply further four hundred thousand 15- or 18-pr. shrapnel shells, empty, packed in ammunition boxes same delivery, price nine and a quarter dollars each, including boxes, not including cost of inspection."
Now, will you tell me (and I am not asking for anything further than the mere fact) were you asked $9.25, which should be $9.25 with 20 cents off for the box, when you told us that you had made up your mind that there would be a profit of $8.55?-A. I will tell you Why. $8.55 inoludes the box.
Q.	Was that the only reason?-A. I don't know, I don't remember that price of $8.55.
Q. It is in Exhibit No. 16?-A. I don't remember that.
Q. On the 18th of September General Hughes , sent to " Troopers " the following: " Reference your cipher September 17th, committee reports price of 100,000 shrapnel 18-pr. as per your cablegram specifications will be $8.55 eaoh delivered at Montreal, 20,000 by November 1st, and at least 30,000 monthly thereafter." Do you remember that?-A. Was that the first one?
Q. That is the first offer I can find as to price?-A. Yes.
Q. And that was on the 18th of September? -A. Yes, sir.
Q. Then " Committee report 100,000 shrapnel price $8.30 each."-A. 15-pr.
Mr. Ewart: Better read it, Mr. Johnston.
Mr. Johnston: Very well. " Committee report 100,000 shrapnel 15-pr. shells." Then there was an acceptance of that price under Exhibit 18 on the 18th of September, but no fuses discussed at all.
Q. That you told us was, as I took it down, you were satisfied there was a profit on that contract?.-A. Just go back now. At the time we realized we were going to get a profit was long after the 18th of September, I said several weeks.
Q. You said that in the end of November you would make up your mind that there would be a profit at $8.55, and you said to-day that long before that you had made up your mind that there would be a profit. You have sworn to it this morning?-A. Well, what about it?
Q. What do you say about it yourself-I am not giving evidence.-A. What is the question?
219J
Q. The question is, that you said yesterday that about the end of November you made up. your mind that there would be a profit at $8.55?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. This morning you said that long before that you had made up your mind that there would be a profit at $8.55?-A. I said that tentatively.
Q. Now, I am asking you how it was that you demanded for the same article $9.05, 70 cents difference on the shell, on the 24th November according to this cable; I want the reason for it?-A. I cannot remember.
Q. You cannot give me any reason for it'____
A. No.
Mr. Ewart: He gave one reason, the boxes?

nobody's business whether they paid to their friends higher prices than they should have paid, nobody's business what they did, nobody's business whether they made a loss or not, so long as they delivered the goods-then I do not think I should have the right to come here. But I have stated to the House that the members of the Shell Committee do not take that attitude. They say that while it is true that they took the legal attitude of being contractors, they always intended to hand this money over, and that they did hand it over, and it went to their successors, the Imperial Munitions Board. I hope I have sufficiently answered the hon. member for West Peterborough; I have tried to make it as plain as I possibly can. In order to arrive at any just conclusion as to the conduct of the members of the old Shell Committee; in order to come to any conclusion as to whether or not they conducted themselves in a proper manner, speaking from the commercial standpoint; in order to satisfy ourselves and the country as to whether these munitions which were bought on account of the British Government, and, according to the statement of the Minister of Finance some months ago, to some extent for the Government of Canada, were purchased as cheaply as they should have been purchased and whether the. transaction was as sound a business transaction as it should have been, I submit, Sir, that the scope of this inquiry should be so enlarged that we should have the Tight to go into the method by which they made up the estimate that they saved $42,000 in the one case, $14,800,000 in the second case, and $30,000,000 in the third case. That is what I want to bring before the House and especially before the Prime Minister, because, being a good lawyer, he can appreciate exactly what I am talking about. I do not go so far as to question the ruling of the commissioners; I want to keep entirely away from that phase of the case. I have tried to place these facts before the House in order that they might be treated by the House entirely as a legal matter, coupled, of course, with the public interest; in order that the matter anight be discussed from that standpoint and not in any way from the standpoint of what may have taken place or what will take place before the Royal Commission. I do not have to remind the House that in my judgment it would be entirely improper to discuss that, and I do not propose doing so, because the Royal Commission is not more than half

Before I take my seat I wish publicly to draw to the attention of the Prime Minister -and I hope that I shall be allowed to do so, even though the matter is not contained in the notice which I gave to you, Mr. Speaker,-the fact that under the terms of the Inquiries Act there is no provision for taking the evidence of a witness outside the Dominion of Canada; that is, there is no provision for compelling the attendance of such witness. You are well aware, Mr. Speaker, that most of the states of the Union have provisions for compelling the attendance of witnesses before commissions issued out of our courts under certain conditions. In the state of New York the statute reads practically in this way-I think I can give it almost verbatim, although I have not the citation before me-I think it is section 915 of the Code of New York: " Any party to a suit, cause or action pending in any court may apply to have commissioners appointed, subject to the procedure afterwards given, which commissioners shall have the right to examine witnesses under oath, ask for and compel the production of documents," and generally to go on and work it out. There are decisions in the state of New York providing that a judge under the procedure granted may subpoena and' force the attendance of witnesses before the commission appointed just the same as would be done in our own courts. There is no provision of our Inquiries Act which brings us within the purview of that sort of condition. That is to say, our Inquiries Act does not recognize the existence of parties; it does not recognize a Commission under our Act to be a court. As I view it, therefore, our Commissioners would have no power to appoint a Commission to go to any state in the Union and compel the attendance of witnesses the same as they could if these were applied for out of a court or by a party to a cause in that court. I make this suggestion to the Prime Minister, with the intention at the earliest possible moment-

The difficulty that he has found-one which, I think, is very obvious to all who consider the question-is this:
The statute, as he has observed, which really requires amendment for this purpose, is that in force in New York. The first information of an important and definite character that came to me with regard to the operations of the Shell Committee was that which I quoted in a speech delivered in this House on the 15th day of April, 1915. The members of the Shell Committee had called upon me with the Minister of Militia shortly before and described the extent of the operations of the Shell Committee and their possible development in the production of munitions in Canada. I asked them at that time to make a written statement which they afterwards prepared and which I read in the House on the 15th April, 1915. And certainly, whatever the legal forais may have been which were observed between the Shell Committee on the one hand and the War Office on the other hand, the memorandum which I then read to the House conveyed to me the most distinct impression, as I am sure it did to all members of the House, that they were acting as a committee and were not acting in a contractual relation. Therefore, that clause was inserted in the Order in Council. We had also in mind this: We proposed to send over to the Government of the United Kingdom the whole debate on the motion proposed by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, with the assurance that if an inquiry into the matter were desired at this stage, we would be prepared to give every possible assistance and co-operation in such inquiry, and that as far as we were concerned the Government of Canada had absolutely no objection to such inquiry. So, the clause in the Order in Council fulfilled a double purpose in that regard.
Thereafter, on the 17th day of April, I read to the House an Order in Council which was .passed on the 15th of April, setting forth in terms the motion proposed by my right hon,. friend the leader of the Opposition with regard to this matter, and my observations in regard to it. Having regard to these considerations and to the statement above quoted, the Prime Minister recommends that the Hansard report of the debate upon the motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier be transmitted to the Right Honourable the Secretary of State for the Colonies, with the assurance that the Government of Canada is prepared to assist and co-operate, as stated by the Prime Minister in the House of Commons, in any inquiry or investigation into the transactions to which reference is made in the motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and that so far as the Government of Canada is concerned there is no objection whatever to the fullest investigation that may be thought desirable at any time.
It is not necessary for me to do more than allude to the reasons which were set forth as to why we declined to enter upon such an inquiry without consultation with the British Government. There were two main reasons: One was that the expenditure was not by the Government of Canada, but by the Government of the United. Kingdom, and another consideration was

this, that during the pxogress of a great war such as that in which we are now engaged, the Government of the United Kingdom might not think it desirable that an inquiry should take place at the present time. I do not think my right hon. friend is stating the position exactly as it is, because, while if these contracts had not been put in in evidence and one side of the case had not been put forward, possibly my hon. friend's contention would be logically right; but Mr. Johnston's main contention was that, as these contracts had been put in evidence, and as the statement had been made about savings, he should have the Tight to crossexamine in order to test out the credibility of the witnesses and see exactly what the results ought to be.

I do not quite see the relation, because the charge made in this House was not in regard to the savings of the committee, that is, the difference between the amount which the British Government had authorized and the amount at which the committee had placed their contracts. The question was as to alleged exorbitant and inordinate profits made with respect to certain fuse contracts and other contracts, coupled with the suggestion, or the insinuation, that these contracts had been brought about through the instigation of the Minister of Militia and through some supposed influence that Mr. J. Wesley Allison had exercised upon him. That was precisely the issue which the hon. member for Richmond and other hon. members on the other side of the House proposed for investigation, and that is precisely the matter which the commissioners are proceeding to investigate, and as to which, so far as I understand, they are giving the fullest opportunities for in-

quiry. Sir William Meredith, further on, in reply to Mr. Johnston, said:
Sir William Meredith: That involves going Into eaeh one of the transactions mentioned in that agreement; only four of them are the subject of this inquiry.
And for the very good reason that in respect of only four of them was there any charge or even insinuation made in this House which affected in any way the status or honour of any member of this Government; and as to these, we promptly challenged inquiry, and have granted it. There now seems to be a disposition to raise some other question and ask for some other inquiry which is not covered by what hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House themselves suggested and asked for when this matter was brought up. Then, the Hon. Mr. Justice Duff goes on:
Hon. Mr. Duff: The particulars of the prices of particular contracts other than these four contracts-
Mr. Johnston: Yes.
Hon. Mr. Duff: That is to say, there is no question of contracts for fuses-
Mr. Johnston: No, I understand that, as far as the fuses are concerned, but the fuses are included with other matters in a contract of the 1st July, 1915, because there was a lump sum of $16.50 as to these four contracting parties, nominally or really contracting parties, and as I pointed out, and as I again point out, that in order to ascertain the exact status of these gentlemen, I ask to be allowed to go into the transaction, and let me make it as general as possible, into the whole transaction which will bear not upon the question of fuses but upon the position which these gentlemen actually occupied towards the War Office or towards anybody else with regard to these contracts or contracts for similar purposes.
Sir William Meredith: I think our ruling is plain, Mr. Johnston; you will proceed having regard to it, please.
Mr. Johnston: I do not know that I can make it clear to myself.
Sir William Meredith said further on:
Sir William Meredith: As X understand what you have said, if there is a full price, $16.50, part of it only the fuse, the ruling would not prevent you going into an inquiry as to the rest of the $16.50, whatever it is.
Hon. Mr. Duff; That is with regard to the five million.
Mr. Johnston: Yes, I understand that.
Further on Mr. Hellmuth makes these observations:
Mr. Hellmuth: In regard to the ruling the questions that are directed towards elucidating the position of the four gentlemen with the War Office, whether they were, although legally contractors, treating themselves as trustees or agents, I do not understand any questions of that kind are ruled out.
Sir William Meredith: Certainly not.
Mr. Hellmuth : Nor any inquiry in regard to any prices or any contracts that were made in
regard to the fuses with the Amerioan Ammunition Company.
Sir William Meredith: Certainly not.
Mr. Hellmuth: But if my learned friend Mr. Johnston wants to ask in regard to another contract or sub-contract made by these four gentlemen with somebody else in relation to a matter which is not covered by the terms of the Order in Council he cannot go into that.
Sir William Meredith: That is the ruling.
Hon. Mr. Duff: Or which has nothing to do with the contract of the five million.
Further on Sir William Meredith observed :
Sir William Meredith: You understand, Mr. Johnston, that with regard to this five million contract, the question of profits made by anybody is open to inquiry.
Mr. Johnston. I understand that.
Hon. Mr. Duff: Not merely, as to the fuses, you know.
Mr. Johnston: Yes. And as to the five million fuses, not merely as the price of fuses but the prices under the sub-contract and so forth.
Hon. Mr. Duff: As to profits, as to fuse contracts, made by anybody. The fuse contracts were-speaking very roughly-an element in the transaction with regard to the five millions and what has been said with regard to other contracts does not apply to the five millions.
Mr. Johnston: I understand that the five millions is open to all investigation and all inspection of papers and all examination that may be deemed necessary.
Under the circumstances, I hardly am able to appreciate the point or cogency of my hon. friend's suggestion that, by reason of anything that has transpired before the commissioners, there should be an amendment or extension of the terms of the Order in Council. The Government determined in the first instance that it could not undertake to authorize or proceed with a general inquiry into shell contracts, except after consultation with the British Government, and after submitting the whole matter to them. Later on, when a charge, or rather, a suggestion or insinuation was made on the other side of the House purporting to connect a member of the Government with contracts in respect of which it was said that inordinate and exorbitant profits had been made, although there was no. direct charge in the ordinary sense, the Government determined that an inquiry ought to be made, and we brought down and laid upon the table of the House the Order in Council authorizing the present inquiry. That is the matter now being investigated and determined before the commissioners; that is the issue which hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House themselves raised; that is the question, in so far as the status of any member of the Government is concerned, which they themselves asked to have determined; and

so far as I can -understand from a perusal of the proceedings before the commissioners, a copy of which I have under my hand, the commissioners have not only granted but are disposed to grant , in the future tlie widest latitude to those who are pressing this inquiry and endeavouring to support the allegations of the hon. member for Richmond. Under the circumstances it does not seem to me that either the Government or the members of this House are called upon to reverse a decision that was made after careful debate in this House, merely for the reason that an honourable member of the Bar, however eminent, may think it suits his purpose for the time being to pursue a particular line of crossexamination. So far as these contracts are concerned, everything is absolutely open to him.
So far as the status of the Shell Committee and its relationship to the War Office is concerned, the commissioners, if I understand their ruling correctly, will permit him to inquire, not only into the four contracts mentioned in the Order in Council, but, in a general way, into all the con tracts; he is not restricted or limited in any way whatsoever. But when he asks the commissioners to allow him the same scope of inquiry that he would have had if the whole proceedings of the Shell Committee had been referred to the commissioners for inquiry, why, naturally, no one would expect that the commissioners could acquiesce in such a course.
Under these circumstances, I can only say to my hon. friend that I do not feel there is any occasion whatever for an extension of the terms of the Order in Council authorizing the inquiry. If the British Government, after consideration of the documents which have been sent forward, should come to the conclusion that a general inquiry is desirable, we shall be most happy to refer that general inquiry to these same commissioners if they are prepared to undertake it; but, until some such desire or wish on their part is suggested to us, it does not seem to me there is any occasion for further action by the Government of Canada. The commissioners, as far as I understand-I have not had time to follow the evidence carefully-are giving, and properly giving, not only a fair but a wide interpretation to the terms of the Order in Council; they are giving a wide latitude to the inquiry. But when my hon. friend the member for Carleton suggests that there 
should be an inquiry into the estimated profits under other contracts, or as to how they were made, or how much the operations of the Shell Committee generally cost the British Government, I, for one, am unable to see how such considerations are relevant.
I for one am unable to agree that such considerations enter into this inquiry, or that they affect the particular question which was raised in this House by the hon. member for Richmond, with the approval of hon. gentlemen opposite. Therefore I must say to my hon. friend that, so far as I am concerned, there appears no reason at present for extending the scope of the Order in Council which authorised this inquiry. -

Mr. Speaker, if my right hon. friend the Prime Minister had confined his observations to a statement that he would not consent to enlarge the scope of the commission, I do not know that I should have felt called upon to make any remarks; but the Prime Minister has said further that the Government had decided to issue a commission to investigate all the charges which in any way connected the Government or any member of the Government with mismanagement so far as the affairs of the Shell Committee were concerned, and then he has said that a perusal of the proceedings before the Royal Commission shows that they are giving the widest possible latitude and that no objection can be made against their proceedings. As to these two positions I desire to take distinct issue with my right hon. friend. I say that there was a distinct charge made against the Shell Committee with which a member of this Government was directly connected; that that charge pertained to the general conduct of the Shell Committee and was not limited to the purchase of fuses. That charge was made by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition in the motion which he made for a committee of this House to investigate the conduct .of the Shell Committee; that charge was reiterated by my hon. friend the member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell); and then we had the statement of the Prime Minister that 'if any member of this House would stand in his place and make a formal charge and take the responsibility of his charge, the Government would grant an investigation. Then I, as a humble member of this Houses, and having a deep sense of the responsibility that rested upon me, did stand in my place and make a charge in

words as plain and clear and explicit as possible, and I took the responsibility of proving that charge, well knowing, if I failed to do so, the punishment that would be meted out to me as ' a member of this House. It is idle for the Prime Minister to say that no charge was made. Let me call your attention, Sir, to Hansard, page 1789, and see what was the charge and whether it was made in plain and explicit terms or not:
I, William Pugsley, a member of this House, in support of the motion now under consideration, standing in my place in this House and on my responsibility as a member of this House, declare and charge that the Shell Committee, appointed by the Minister of Militia and referred to in said motion, fixed excessive and unreasonable prices for shells and for other munitions and goods to be furnished to the British Government (which by arrangement between the British Government and the Canadian Government were to be paid for in part by Canada.)
That such prices were fixed with competition and were far in excess of what would necessarily have been paid if ordinary business methods had been pursued, thereby involving an unnecessary excessive expenditure of many millions of dollars, conservatively estimated at at least eighty millions, which will be improperly taken from the people of the United Kingdom and Canada.
That said committee gave large orders at such excessive prices and without competition to companies in which members of the committee were largely interested, and of some of which companies merfibers of the said committee were the directing heads.
There is a charge, not (Confined to the purchase of fuses, but connected with the purchase by the committee of all goods for the purposes of the British Government. Later on in the charge which I made it is expressly declared that the actions of the Shell Committee were known to and were connived at by the Minister of Militia; and yet the Prime Minister says there was no charge connecting any member of this Government with improper conduct, Are we to understand that it will not be deemed a charge against this Government that they are guilty of negligence, that they are guilty by careless business methods, of allowing money to be taken out of the treasury of Great Britain and the treasury of Canada, and that, in order to make a charge against the Administration, you must charge personal dishonesty against some member of the Government? I have never understood that to be the rule applied to men in public life. I directed a charge against this Shell Committee, created by a member of this Government and acting for a member of this Government, that they, neglecting ordinary business methods and disregarding those
ordinary rules of prudence which should guide the gentlemen who are carrying on the affairs of the country, paid excessive prices involving an unnecessary expenditure amounting to the enormous sum of $80,000,000; that that was done with the knowledge and connivance of the Minister of Militia to whom the Shell Committee reported from week to week. It astonishes me that the Prime Minister, in the face of that charge, rises to-day in his place and repeats the statement which he made some time ago in this House, that there was no charge in any way connecting any member of this Government with improper conduct so far as the Shell Committee was concerned. I charged further:
That there has been great and wholly unnecessary delay in furnishing the completed shells for use of the Canadian and British forces at the front.
That the said Shell Committee neglected and delayed for an undue period of time to provide the fuses necessary to render the shells effective, and, failing to endeavour to provide for their construction in Canada, as they might have done, proceeded to give and awarded, through J. Wesley Allison in the United States, contracts for fuses amounting to ?22,000,00o[ on which they made an advance of $3,750,OOo! That the making of the said contracts through said Allison was unwise and improvident and was entered into with the knowledge and connivance of the Minister of Militia, and the said Shell Committee failed to obtain * delivery of said fuses for an unreasonable time.
And I do also charge that the Government of Canada had, through the Minister of Militia, to whom the said Shell Committee reported weekly, knowledge of such irregular and improper methods and acts of the said Shell Committee, and while having the power at any time to put an end thereto the said minister improperly consented to such irregular and improper methods and acts and permitted the same to continue.
There was a charge directed against the Shell Committee, not limited to the purchase of fuses, but having refer-
4 p.m. emce to the various actions of that committee in the purchase of shells, shell boxes, and other materials, and charging them with improper and irregular conduct, and that such conduct upon their part was with the knowledge and connivance of the Minister of Militia.	Yet my right hon.
friend says there was no charge against the Shell Committee so far as any member of the Government being connected with it was concerned, except in reference to fuses, and that the latter charge was made by my hon. friend the member for Richmond. 1 feel constrained to make that statement in view of what my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has said in reference to there being no charge connecting any mem-

ber of this Government with improper conduct.
The Prime Minister says that they have not dealt with this matter as if this committee had any contractual relations with the Imperial Government, but as if they were a committee. Does he forget that he and the members of this Government informed this House and informed the people that this Shell Committee was in no way responsible to this Government or to any member of this Government, but that all this Government did was to name seven reputable gentlemen for selection by the British Government as their committee for the purchase of munitions of war, and that it was to the British Government, and to the British Government alone, that that committee was responsible, that it was with that Government alone that they had relations? Does the Prime Minister forget that? Does the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) forget that? Does the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) forget that? If the Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) were here, he might perhaps say something in a different way; but these gentlemen to whom I have referred, one after another,' stood in their places in the House and said that this Government had nothing in the world to do with this committee. Did my right hon, friend the Prime Minister, when he made that statement in the House, know of these contracts which had been signed by Sir Sam Hughes, Minister of Militia, on the one side, and these four gentlemen, members of the committee, on the other? I cannot believe he knew of them. I cannot believe that had he known of them he would have concealed them from the knowledge of the members of this House and of the people of Canada. Some may think it strange that he did not know of these contracts, for they had seen it reported in the newspapers that at times he was acting Minister of Militia. It may seem strange to hon. members of this House that other gentlemen did not know of them, for we have seen the statement made at one time that the President of the Council, Mr. Lougheed, was acting Minister of Militia. Other gentlemen from time to time have acted as Minister of Militia. Some may think it strange that, taking charge of the department as they did, none should know of the' existence of these contracts which, it has been said, had been so much a surprise when evidence of them was disclosed before the Royal Commission. These contracts were, as I have said, directly between these four 
gentlemen and this Government, through its Minister of Militia. Will it be said, in view of these contracts being now before the country, that this committee had nothing to do with this Government? Will it be said that they had nothing to do with the Minister of Militia? Will it be said that the Minister of Militia was not the man who took these orders from the British Government and then gave orders to these gentlemen who did so make the contracts? To-day we have the facts, we have the absolute confirmation of the statement of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) made in, this House when he quoted the remarks of Lord Curzon that these orders came directly from the War Office to the Minister of Militia of Canada. When that statement was made, hon. gentlemen on the other side were disposed to question it, but to-day we have the fullest confirmation of the position which the leader of the Opposition took in proposing his motion to the House.
The Prime Minister says that it is evident that there is no necessity for enlarging the scope of the commission, that it is evident . the commission has been given the freest hand that any counsel can in reason ask to be given them. I am not disposed to agree with my right hon. friend in that. In a court of law, if the counsel for the plaintiff were to put in a document and examine the witness upon that document, whether the document was relevant or irrelevant, the counsel upon the other side would have the right to cross-examine with regard to that document. I ask any lawyer in this House if that would not be the case. That is one of the clearest and most elementary principles of daw. Yet we find that the, gentleman representing this Government and taking his instruction from this Government puts in these various documents, puts in the calculations of profits, and, with the consent of the commissioners, went fully and with very great detail into the actions of the Shell Committee so far as it pleased him to do so, but that, when Mr. Johnston proposed to crossexamine on these very documents the statement which Mr. Hellmuth, representing the Government, had placed before the Committee, he was denied the right to cross-examine, a right which would have been accorded to counsel in any court in this country. Does my Tight hon. friend the Prime Minister, as a lawyer of great

ability and large experience, say that that is fair play? Does he say that one side should be permitted to put in such documents as it pleases and that counsel representing a different interest shall not be permitted to cross-examine upon those documents? I deny that that is in accordance with the principles that govern ordinary legal proceedings; I deny that that is in accordance with the principles which should govern the Commission if they are desirous of having the fullest investigation and of the facts going to the public. If the Prime Minister does not feel like granting the request of my hon. friend from Carleton that the scope of the Commission should be enlarged, he should instruct Mr. Hellmuth, acting for the Government, to permit the fullest cross-examination upon all matters which he went into in his direct examination That would be only fair play, that would be only in accordance with justice and with the rules of procedure, which, as every lawyer knows, govern the taking of evidence in the courts of this country.
Just a word with reference to the suggestion of my hon. friend from Carleton that the Government should introduce legislation so as to give these judges, who are appointed under Royal Commission, the status of a court, in order that they may have power to issue a commission to the United States, and so be enabled to obtain evidence in that country. My hon. friend recognizes the desirability of doing that if it can be done. It is known that this very large contract was given in the United States; it is known that some of the most important witnesses reside in the United States; it is known that these witnesses cannot be compelled by any process to come to this country and that the only way in which their evidence can be secured would be by some procedure which would enable them to be brought before a representative of the commission in the United States. If the Government does not lend its aid-if that aid can be made effective towards this result-it would be putting a premium upon those acting for this Government going to the United States and there making their contracts, carrying on their business, and spending the money of this Government-or the money entrusted to the Shell Committee which is in reality the money of this Government and the money of Great Britain-because they would expect that no commission could follow them into a foreign oountry and obtain evidence which would be available if the transaction had been carried on in Canada. I hope my right hon. friend the
Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice will bend their energies toward giving such a constitution to this commission as will prevent it from being deprived of the opportunity of taking the testimony of witnesses in the United States. It is admitted that if these commissioners were a court they could issue a commission to the United States and witnesses would be obliged to attend. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice has eaid that that can only be done in a proceeding either civil or criminal. Well, no one pretends that it is a criminal proceeding that these commissioners are carrying on; but is it not a civil proceeding?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Some very uncivil
things have been said about it.

I do not think so. We on this side of the House, while we regret that. a committee of the House was not appointed to investigate this matter, and while the inquiry has not been broad so as to take in all the matters with respect to which we made these most serious charges, recognize that half a loaf is better than no bread, and that if opportunity is given for full inquiry it will be, to some extent at all events, satisfactory to the public. Why could not an Act he passed declaring that these commissioners shall be deemed to be a court of inquiry? Why should a clerk to this court not be appointed, and why should it not be provided that that court, so constituted-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me a question? Can this Parliament legislate that a body shall be deemed a court, and make that effective in the state of New York if the body is not a court?

Yes. The moment this Parliament, having jurisdiction to create a court for inquiry irtto public affairs, constitutes that body a court with power to take evidence under oath, to punish witnesses for contempt and to issue commissions to a foreign country, at that moment it becomes a court which will be recognized by the laws of a foreign country, the courts of which will then lend their aid to the bringing of witnesses before a commissioner appointed by our court to hear evidence. Does my hon. friend doubt the power of this Parliament to constitute a court? Only two days ago my hon. friend introduced a Bill to amend the Exchequer Court Act, in which he pro-



poe-es that the court shall carry on investigations and make inquiries even though they are not to pronounce judgment taking away property from the individual and giving it to the Crown. They are to carry on investigation and report to the Government as to the value of the property in regard to which they make the investigation. Suppose that was the whole power of the Exchequer Court; suppose it had not the power to give judgment, but were appointed simply for the purpose of making inquiry with regard to property which the Crown had expropriated and to report to the Government upon the value of the property. It would be equally a court; it could be equally given power to compel witnesses to come before it, to administer oaths, to punish for contempt. Equally could it be given the power to issue commissions to a foreign country in case it should be desirable to take evidence in such foreign country. I do not think my hon. friend will question the validity of the legislation thait he himself is proposing with regard to the Exchequer Court. If that is so, then what is the difficulty in constituting these two judges a court of inquiry under the Inquiries Act? What is to prevent this Parliament from giving to the court so constituted the power to compel witnesses to attend before them, to punish for contempt, to employ. all the powers of a court? What is to hinder this Parliament from giving that court power to issue a commission to a foreign, country? If this Government will do that, I venture to say that we shall not require any amendment to the law of New York. I venture to say that upon application to a judge of the Supreme Court of New York an order will be made for the attendance of witnesses before the commissioner which the court so -constituted may .appoint. That is all the hon. member for Carleton asks for; that is what this Parliament has the power to grant if the Government choose to take that course, and if they desire that witnesses in the United States shall tell what they know about these facts. I am told that witnesses in the United States will be able to give the most valuable evidence with regard to the charges which have been made. That, I say, is the course which this Government ought to take if they are desirous of having a full and complete and thorough investigation and of having all the facts disclosed by this Royal Commission.
[Mr. Pugsley.I

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when my right hon.
friend the leader of the House closed his observations, I confess that I felt at that moment that there required nothing to be added to what he said in order to justify the conclusion at,which he arrived and to demonstrate that there was no basis for the demand for the enlargement of this commission. I feel that I should apologize to this House for rising now to speak, because I have had such a strong confirmation of that view in the speech of the hon. member for St. John city (Mr. Pugsley). Assuredly, if there had been something to be said that would tend to support the claim that at this stage and for the purpose suggested by the hon. member for Carleton the scope of this commission should be extended, I think we might have counted upon the hon. member for St. John to find it out. But apparently he has deemed it necessary to confine his observations almost entirely to matters which, so far as I can see, do not bear upon the question of the extension of the scope of this commission.
He made complaint that the right hon. Prime Minister had stated that no charges other than those under investigation affecting any member of this Government had been made in this House. He proceeded to read to us some extracts from a speech which he had made in the course of the debate upon the motion of the right hon. leader of the Opposition for an inquiry before a committee, and he told us that these were charges. If the use of the word " charges " made them charges in any proper sense of the word, I think it could not be disputed that they were charges, because he repeated the word " charges " in almost every paragraph. The hon. gentleman -seemed to have almost extraordinary conception of the effect of the use of the word. We have an instance of that in another portion of his argument, where he gravely represents to us that if we just call a body a court, that makes it a court and there is nothing more to be said about it-all outside states will recognize it as being a court. I do not attach the same value to words that the hon. gentleman does; in that connection I will have something to say further on.
I do' not purpose going into the question of these so-called charges. At the time that they were made, even with greater solemnity than they have been read to-day, my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) very fully and very adequately

disposed of them. I want to refer only to one paragraph of them, the one that comes nearest to accusing someone of something. It is the paragraph in which these contracts of $22,000,000 are dealt with, and I want to refer to that only to point out that these are the contracts that are now under investigation
The hon. gentleman gets up to contradict the right hon. leader of the House in his statement that no charges other than those under investigation were made, and he cites the charge that is under investigation.

Will my hon. friend
pardon me? My information is, and I have not the shadow of a doubt about it, that the contracts put in by Mr. Hellmuth are not limited to fuses at all, but contain the contracts in regard to the shells as well as the fuses.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: How does that bear on what I am stating, namely, that the charges with regard to contracts for $22,000,000 are under investigation? The hon. gentleman rises to say that not only are they under investigation, but that other matters are under investigation; and yet the gist of his complaint was that he made charges and that they were not under investigation.

My hon. friend persists in misrepresenting me. What I said was that the counsel for the Government put in all those contracts, not limiting them to the fuse contracts, and then Mr. Johnson was deprived of the privilege of crossexamining upon the matters into which the Government counsel had examined in the direct examination.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We will come to that in a moment; we have not come near it yet. The hon. gentleman accuses me of misrepresenting him; but if he will keep his mind on what I am dealing with at the moment, I do not think he will venture to deny that what he describes as a charge and what approximates most nearly to a charge in his very-I may be pardoned if I say verbose and numerous statements intended to look like charges-what comes nearest to a charge and looks most like one, is actually under investigation now.

My statement is only
verbose as compared with the brief speeches of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That may be; I do not know whether I am subject to the reproach
220i
ox too great brevity. However, that is all I have to say about his charges. The nearest approach to a charge is actually under investigation, and the hon. gentleman takes up our time complaining that the right hon. gentleman has said that no charges other than those under investigation have been made. I entirely fail to see the bearing of the fact that the hon. gentleman made what he called charges upon the question whether this commission, having been issued to inquire into an issue tendered by the hon. gentleman upon the other side of the House, should now be extended to cover all of the contracts of the Shell Committee. The hon. gentlemen who made these charges which have been subjected to investigation were exceedingly brave when they made them. Their words were many and their words were brave, and they clamoured for a body before which they ( could make the proof of those specific things that are now under investigation; they have a body before which they are given the widest possible latitude concerning those charges which they so made, and are furthermore told that they may refer to any other contract in so far as it bears upon the status of the Shell Committee, and what do they do? I have not read the evidence and I do not want to draw any conclusion from it, but it does not seem very unfair to suggest that it looks at all events like running away from the issue that they tendered. They are given the widest possible latitude on the issue they tendered, and they are here before this House complaining that they are not allowed to go into something else, and all of that because they say, if I followed the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., aright, that there is a question of the status of the committee, and, in the second place, because there is in the evidence a statement showing that large savings were effected as between the prices agreed upon by the War Office and the prices at which contracts were actually made

Does the minister
lay it down as a principle that in this tribunal or in any other court where counsel acting for a party having responsibility introduces evidence to show that there were profits or savings or whatever you choose to call them, the counsel on the other side cannot cross-examine in regard to that fact? That is the ruling here in the minutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I venture to say so, and I say it is fortified by the ruling of the Chief Justice of Ontario and of Mr. Justice Duff,

one of the most distinguished judges on the Supreme Court Bench, which ruling is absolutely at variance with the suggestion the hon. member for Pictou has just made, and the suggestion which the hon. member for St. John made. The hon. member for St. John said he ventured to say that there was not a lawyer of any standing in this country who would question his proposition, and yet his proposition was in thie teeth of the ruling of the Chief Justice of Ontario and of Mr. Justice Duff.

I am putting that
to you as a general principle. What do you say about it?
What does the minister himself say?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What the minister says is that if, as has been held, these contracts are irrelevant to the matter to be inquired into, the fact that there had been introduced a statement showing the profits made by them, a statement introduced, so far as1 we know, without the slightest objection on anybody's part, does not make that statement a relevant statement pertinent to the inquiry, and consequently gives no right to cross-examine upon it. The suggestion of these two hon. gentlemen amounts to this, that if I should sue a man on a contract for $500, and I should go into the witness box and, in the course of my testimony, voluntarily observe that I made another contract and realized $10,000 profit at some other time, because that evidence had slipped in, because nobody has said anything about it going in, then the court would be called upon to investigate my statement, which has no bearing on my case at all, that I made $10,000 in some other contract at some other time.
Would the minister say that in that very case there would be no right of cross-examination?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly and most absolutely I would say so.
There must be something different in the Quebec code from what is in the common law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen laugh. If they were in a court I think the laughing would be at their expense.

I think you had better
look for some other illustration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
For what my capacity
may be, I have not the slightest hesitation
TMr. Doherty.]
in saying and I feel somewhat fortified by the fact that this is the ruling of Chief Justice Meredith and of Mr. Justice Duff-

Does not the minister's logic go to this extent, that if the decision of the Chief Justice of Ontario on this question is right, he should not have permitted the evidence in regard to shell savings or profits to go into the record before the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So far as contracts are concerned, the contracts between the Shell Committee and the Imperial Government were put in at the beginning, for the purpose, as I understand it,-and I am depending largely on the statements of the hon. member for Carleton which I have no doubt reproduces what happened, although there may be room for differences of impression-

I do not think so, I
think you are pretty safe in accepting it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I take it that those
contracts were put in to show the status as towards the War Office of the Shell Committee, and I understand a statement was put in, and, so far as I am informed, without anybo'dy suggesting objection to it, that showed, in a general way, that a saving had been effected upon the prices at which the sub-contracts were let.
It dropped there. I do not know what would have been the ruling if it had been objected to; but this much is quite clear, that the two learned judges have ruled that cross-examination, going into the details of what profits were made on each one of these contracts, is not justified by the introduction of the statement, and that it is irrelevant to the matters being inquired into. I think it would not be unwise of this House to. leave that matter to be determined by these two learned judges. There will not be much gained by my quarrelling with my hon. friends on the other side of the House as to whether this is a sound judgment or not. I am quite prepared, and I think that other hon. members of this House will also be, to abide by the decision of the commissioners on that question, and that is their judgment.
If one follows the argument of Mr. Johnston, it is apparent that he claims to go into these contracts as bearing upon the status of the Shell Committee towards the War Office. The declaration of the commissioners on the subject has been read here more than once, that in so far as they may be pertinent to establish that

status they may be gone into. The other assertion is the one I have just dealt with, namely, that because there happened to be a statement that these profits were made, although these profits have absolutely nothing to do with the issue that the commission was appointed to try, we ought to extend the scope of the commission in order to enable them to go into all the contracts made by the Shell Committee. I am not going into the question whether that should be done or not. That question was threshed out in this House on the motion of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

On another suppose^
state of affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In what respect?
On the supposition that the Shell Committee were trustees instead of contractors.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not going into the question of whether they are in effect trustees or contractors. If I followed the hon. gentleman rightly, his contention was that legally, on the letter of the instrument, they were contractors.
There is no doubt about that at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Very well; I am not
questioning that; but they themselves say that morally they were representatives or trustees.
But with the right to pay any amount which they had a mind to for these articles so long as it did not exceed the estimated cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That matter might
very well be left to the commissioners to determine.
Yes. I do not wish to discuss it here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What their rights are
may be left to the commissioners to determine; but how does that affect the question of the scope of the commission? The commissioners have told Mr. Johnston that, as far as anything bears on the question of the status of the Shell Committee, he may go into it. There can be no dispute about that question. All that has been ruled out is the details, the particulars, of the different sub-contracts which these parties made, other than the sub-contracts referred to in, the commission, because they are all
sub-contracts in this sense, in regard to fuses. That is all that has been ruled out. All I have seen, as a vestige of ground for suggesting that all these other contracts should go in, is the mere fact of the exist-[DOT]cnce of that statement. I have dealt with that argument, and it seems to me that it requires no further observation.
The hon. member for St. John, taking up a suggestion of the hon. member for Carle-ton and harking back on something that was said by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald)-if I might be permitted to refer to something that was mentioned in a previous debate-calls upon the Government, and upon myself in a very particular manner, to legislate to make this commission of inquiry a court which will be recognized in the United States as being a court. He says that all I have to do in order to bring about that result is to give that body the powers of a court in regard to the summoning of witnesses, the examining of witnesses and compelling attendance, and to give them power to issue commissions themselves to other persons. May I point out to him that under the statute at present these are precisely the powers that this body has, and that the only modification he has suggested is that we should call this body a court. I would like to refer to the statute of the state of New York and to our own statute upon that subject. I do so simply for the purpose of making it perfectly clear that statutes of that sort are passed in order to enable courts of different countries to act in aid of each other, if I may so express it. I have here only the statute of the state of New York, but I feel fairly safe in saying that you will find the statutes of other countries on the subject are similar. They all have in contemplation a court, that is to say, a tribunal sitting for the administration of justice and holding trials between parties and carrying on proceedings either civil or criminal. The provision of the New York statute is:
A party to an action, suit, or special proceeding, civil or criminal, pending in a court without the State, either in the United States, or in a foreign country, may obtain, by the special proceeding prescribed in this article, the testimony of a witness-
And so forth. The details of the procedure are immaterial. The right is given to a party in action, suit, or special proceeding, civil or criminal, pending in a 'court; so that you must have a court, you must have a proceeding to which there are

parties, and it must be a proceeding civil or criminal. With all respect to the hon. member for St. John, when he suggests that in a legal sense, and within the well-known meaning which the words have, as distinguishing between a civil and a criminal proceeding, this is a civil proceeding, I find it impossible to follow him. This is an inquiry directed to the ascertaining of facts. Upon the results of that inquiry a civil or criminal proceeding may be based; but we are at present at the stage when we have not got the material upon which to base a proceeding, civil or criminal. Our own statute, making a similar provision in favour of outside courts, is very much in the same terms:
Whenever, upon an application for that purpose, it is made to appear to any court or judge, that any court or tribunal of competent jurisdiction, in any other of His Majesty's dominions-
This one deals with His Majesty's other dominions, but there is a provision in regard to foreign countries-
__before which any civil, commercial or criminal
matter is pending, is desirous of obtaining.-
Etc. We might call this a court if we chose, but it would not alter in any sense its functions; and as long as there is instituted before it no action or proceeding, and it is not competent to entertain any action or proceeding, none of these statutes will apply. If we were in a position to proceed before any court and institute any action or proceeding, we would not need to go before this commission at all. There are ample courts in this country if anybody has charges to make. Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House said there were charges to bring, said they were in possession of evidence that would convict men under the Criminal Convictions Act-
Who made that statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot at the moment lay my hands on it.
