The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) came the nearest to it.
Mr. CARVELL': I think the minister should be a little more specific. If he will exclude me I shall not find so much fault.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the statement is questioned I will drop it, but I have sat here and heard appeals made to the Minister

of Justice, " Why do-n't you prosecute the man for perjury?" When I used the words "criminal convictions," I realized I was not using the right words; I should have said, under the " Secret Commissions Act."
That is a different proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would suggest that if hon. gentlemen had that evidence and wanted a tribunal to compel the attendance of witnesses, they should have gone to the courts of this country to lay their charges, and then they would have had the assistance of courts of other countries to compel the attendance of the witnesses wanted. When they refused that remedy, what was it they asked for in the same breath? They asked for a committee of this House, which manifestly and unquestionably would have had no greater power than this commission; would not have had the powers that a constituted court would have of compelling the attendance of witnesses. I was surprised when it was first suggested by the hon. member for Pictou; but, as the suggestion had been made by a gentleman for whose professional status I have the greatest respect, I made it my business to look into the matter as carefully as I could, and I am free to confess that for the reasons I have pointed out I think it is beyond our power. But if any method can be devised to compel the attendance of witnesses before this commission-whether it is called a court of inquiry or anything else-hon. gentlemen may rest assured that that method will be resorted to. They need have no doubt about our desire to do everything that can be done to bring before the commission witnesses that it is desired to examine, on all matters that are pertinent to the investigation being carried on.
If it is to be in the form of a statute, it should be passed before Parliament rises.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am free to admit that the hon. gentleman is a distinguished lawyer, and he knows or he does not know whether we can pass a statute of that kind. Personally, I know of no legislation that could be enacted. We cannot alter the real nature of the body, we cannot alter the real nature of the proceedings, by any legislation of ours that will be effective in the United States. We may legislate that a something that is not a court shall

be a court in Canada; but that would not carry in the United States, because we should only be giving the body a name. We have a body whose functions are essentially not those of a court, because the commissioners can impose no consequences upon people by reason of the findings of facts that they may make; they have no judicial function in that sense to exercise: they, therefore, are not a court or tribunal within the meaning of any of those statutes, and our calling them so will not create against people who are governed by the law of the United States rights that do not exist under the law of the United States or of the particular states in which the people may be found. We can neither make this a court that would be recognized in the United States, by merely calling it a court; nor can we make this a proceeding, civil or criminal, by merely calling it so, in such a manner as to have that recognized in the United States. If hon. gentlemen can suggest any method by which that can be done, I shall be more than happy to accept it. There is certainly an element of inconsistency in hon. gentlemen who would have nothing but a committee of Parliament to inquire into these charges complaining of the lack -of power of this commission to enforce the attendance of witnesses. This commission has already, so far as the law of Canada can give it, all the powers of a court to enforce the attendance of witnesses.
Would not a committee of Parliament have the same power?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What is suggested to
me is that a court would have more power. What I say is that this commission has all the powers of a court with regard to the enforcement of the attendance of witnesses.
In Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes; and so has a court in Canada. What power they may have outside of Canada depends upon the statutes of the country in which the power is sought to be exercised, and not upon our legislation. If the reasoning of the hon. member for St. John is correct, I would' say that the State of New York ought to. recognize this body as being a court, because it has been given, in regard to the inquiry, all the powers of a court. But I do not think that foreign (States would recognize it as being a court, and I do not think they would be any more likely to do so if we called- it a court. I am sorry to have detained the House so long, but
I wanted to explain this matter with regard to the existence of the powers attached to this commission, and the possibility of our widening those powers. If that possibility exists I shall be more than happy to avail myself of it.
But to come back to the real question that is at issue, I must confess that I can see no ground suggested for an extension of the commission other than the mere fact that this statement has been placed on the record; and the conclusion drawn from that, that we are. therefore to go into the minutiae of all those contracts, because, perhaps irrelevantly, the sum total of savings has gone on the record, seems to me a proposition absolutely untenable, and its consequences, I think, demonstrate that. If the conclusion were correct, then the accident of the going on the record of any irrelevant statement would open up in this inquiry- and would open up in any case-any number of cases that might happen to be referred to in that irrelevant statement. I think the conclusive) condemns the prop jsition. Upon the whole I entirely fail to see what case has been made for the extension of this commission. And might I add that, if there were room to suggest that we ought to take up further cases, would it not be reasonable to dispose, first of all, of the case we have? ' Why do hon. gentlemen think it so necessary to- get away from the case that is really before the commission, and with regard to which the doors are absolutely wide open, and at this stage, before that case is disposed of, want to run into an investigation of every other contract that was made by the Shell Committee? Surely, if the time ever comes when there will be occasion to do that, we shall be none the worse off for having at least dealt with and determined the one case which was put forward as the typical and the gravest case- the case upon which hon. gentlemen seemed disposed to stake their all in connection with their endeavour to cast reflection upon this Government by means of their accusations against the Shell Committee.

The question involved in -the matter brought before the House by my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) is one which it seems to me ought to have met with a more favourable reception from the Government.
In the course of the proceedings had before the tribunal called under the Inquiries Act by this Government for the purpose of investigating certain matters relating to
t

fuse contracts, referred to them by the Government, the counsel appointed by this Government proceeded to put in evidence certain documents and facte relative to the constitution of the Shell Committee and to the contracts entered into by them in connection with the manufacture of shells, which were not, strictly speaking, the subject matter of the charge. In the course of tendering that evidence and bringing that matter before the commission, Mr. Hellmuth, counsel for the Government, produced certain contracts and elucidated certain facts relative to the manufacture of shells, as we see in the-report of the proceedings of the tribunal as, for instance, whether basic steel should be used, 'and so on. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice, who speaks about hon. gentlemen on this side wanting to go into the examination of the question of shells, forgets entirely that that tribunal, which is created by the Government of which my hon. friend is a member, permitted the Government counsel to raise that question. When, however, Mr. Johnston, who was also appointed by the Government, for the purpose, I presume, of cross-examining witnesses and placing before the public all the matters connected with the inquiry, following out what he deemed to be his duty, asked certain questions relative to shell contracts and to the way in which those contracts were carried out, the tribunal said: "That is not within pur reference, and therefore we will not permit you to go on." I think that is a fair statement of the matter, as I gather it from the report of the proceedings. Apprehending that the situation created might be considered a singular one, Sir William Meredith, the presiding judge of the tribunal, suggested that this House should be approached in regard to the matter. He said:
You are aware, of course, the Order in Council provides for the reference of other questions to this commission if it is thought expedient to do so. If anybody thinks that these matters ought to be inquired into, and we are to stay here all summer doing it, I suppose representations can be made. Mr. Carvell is a member of the House, he can bring the matter up and ask that the power of the inquiry be extended.
In consequence of the suggestion of Sir William Meredith, the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., came here, and I think the House will agree with me that he stated fairly the matters connected with the suggestion and the reasons why that suggestion should be accepted by the Govem-

ment. When hon. members on this side point out that an anomaly is created by virtue of documents and other evidence being admitted in relation to shells in regard to which no cross-examination is permitted, my hon. friend the Minister of Justice affects to believe that it is an astounding principle to assert that the right of cross-examination ought not to be limited in such a case. With all deference to my hon. friend's legal standing, I am bound to say that I have never heard it stated in any court that, when documents 5 p.m. are permitted to be gone into by the examining counsel, the cross-examiner must not deal with them. You may say that those facts were not relevant. If so, why was the examining counsel permitted to examine in regard to them? If the position is taken that crossexamination in regard to certain facts was not permitted because those facts were irrelevant, the proper course would have been not to have admitted those facts in the first instance. Mr. Johnston says, at page 373:
I may say that the question of what took place as gathered from various witnesses may be important from our standpoint, from my standpoint at any rate, and I so submitted at the time; in addition to that the contracts have been proved and they are before the commission, and surely it is open to me to examine as to the contracts proved by my learned friend Mr. Hellmuth, and made part of the record. If they can be proved and nothing more said about it then of course my duty is very simple, as I should not ask if the commissioners so rule, and I would not even attempt to lead up to that.
In answer to a further objection he says:
I answer that by saying that the question of relationship having been asked yesterday and emphasized with General Bertram as to whether or not they were contractors or mere trustees or agents-
The question asked by Mr. Hellmuth, counsel for the Government.
-or whatever one may choose to call them that that question depends entirely upon what was done under these contracts after they were entered into, and facts connected with the contracts themselves and with the action of this witness or any other witness, ought to be avail-[DOT]able to me for the purpose of showing what the real relationship was notwithstanding the evidence my learned friend offered yesterday in regard to the fact that they were not in reality contractors, but agents.
It was because Mr. Johnston desired to dc that which he has indicated in the statement I have read, and because it was ruled by the commission that he could not ask those questions, that the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., came to this House, in

accordance with the suggestion of Sir William Meredith whose suggestion seems to be a very reasonable one, and one which ought to be accepted by this Government.
Does the hon. gentleman insist that that is' a fair statement of the case?

If my hon. friend
does not think it a fair statement, he can answer it when I get through. My hon. friend's interjections in regard to matters about which he knows nothing have become very tiring in this House. If he wants to answer me, let him do so later. I have stated what is in the record; I have stated the facts, and the point is, is anything to be done in regard to the matter?
The position taken by the Government was this, that the Shell Committee were the trusted confidants of the British Government, their creation, their agents, and that to the British Government alone were they responsible. On that basis the matter was discussed in this House and the House voted. After the reference was had, counsel for the Government, by the production of contracts which are the very basis of this discussion, elucidated the fact that the members of the Shell Committee were not the agents of the British Government, were not their appointees, but were simply and solely contractors with them, and that the question as to what was to be done with the surplus left after paying for certain shells was a matter of doubt. It was doubtful whether the money belonged to the members of the Shell Committee or not; and a discussion was had as to whether the money should be given to the Patriotic Fund or returned to the War Office. In other words, the whole position of the Government with regard to the Shell Committee has been absolutely and totally reversed as a result of the facts elucidated by Mr. Hellmuth, as admitted by the right hon. Premier in his speech to-day. The whole point is whether the Government will, m view of those changed conditions, permit Mr.. Johnston, as counsel appointed by themselves for the purpose of elucidating the truth, to crossexamine upon the points which are set out in the proceedings here, and enable him to ask all proper questions with regard to the evidence which has been adduced by Mr. Hellmuth, counsel for the Government. Either the Government will do that or they will not do it. They can refuse, and to that extent the inquiry will be ineffectual and incomplete, and the portion of the evidence that has been adduced by Mr. Hellmuth, the whole evidence not being elucidated, the whole ground not being covered, will, to that extent, be unsatisfactory. About that there can be no doubt whatever. Apparently the Government have taken the position that they do not propose to allow that matter to be gone into, nor to allow Mr. Johnston to undertake that cross-examination which he has indicated.
In this connection, another question has arisen: whether or not the powers of this tribunal created under the Inquiries Act are sufficiently wide to enable them to deal with the taking of evidence outside of the Dominion of Canada. To the suggestion made on that subject the Minister of Justice replied that this is neither a civil proceeding nor a criminal proceeding, and that being neither it does not come within the provision of the New York statute, that being the state within whose bounds witnesses are to be sought. But it may be that the witnesses will not always be in the state of New York. It may be that some of them will cross the river into New Jersey, and there they might be reached by the long arm of a Canadian court. And we have not heard the Minister of Justice discuss what may be the law of New Jersey in regard to taking evidence before a foreign tribunal. This much the Government can do-they can create a court for this particular purpose, endowed with all the powers of a court, and there (being before that court a proceeding within the meaning of the statute cited by the Minister of Justice, you have a tribunal under which, I submit, some way would be found to secure recognition in the United States and in the several states under the Acts there in force. Power to do this, it is conceded, will be found in section 101 of the British North America Act, which is as follows:
The Parliament of Canada may, notwithstanding anything in this Act, from time to time, provide for the constitution, maintenance and organization of a general court of appeal for Canada-
-that is, the Supreme Court.
-and for the establishment of any additional courts for the better administration of the laws of Canada.
" For the better administration of the laws of Canada." The Minister of Justice would be doing only that which he ought to do, if, instead of acting under this totally

inadequate Inquiries Act, he should introduce into this Parliament a statute providing for the constitution of a court with all the powers of a court, to deal with this particular matter. It could then proceed in the way indicated by my hon. friend from St. John, and could take advantage of the statutes of foreign countries, to the extent of which those statutes exist, for the procuring of evidence there.
The Minister of Justice says: "We will not appoint a court, because I find that the New York statute, which I construe in a certain way, limits the right of taking evidence." The hon. gentleman takes the responsibility for that, of course. A peculiar situation arises under the Inquiries Act, as amended by chapter 8 of the statutes olf 1912. It is provided that the commission may allow any person whose conduct is under investigation to be represented by counsel. But I can find no power here given to permit the party making the charge before that tribunal to be represented by counsel. If at any moment this tribunal,' appointed under this Act, should choose to say to Mr. Kyte, for instance, "We do not propose to permit you to go on with this matter, because, while we can appoint counsel to assist us and can appoint counsel for the defence, no particular statutory power is given for the appointment of any one to represent the party making the charge," they would have the power to do so. That is an illustration of the wholly inadequate nature of this court-no, it is not a court, this tribunal-which has been erected for this inquiry. The tribunal is without power to go beyond the borders of Canada to take evidence or to appoint a commission for that purpose. And the position of the Government in regard to this matter is that it has refused to give the tribunal this power.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman states that we have refused to give this tribunal the status we ought to give them of a court within the powers of the statute of New York. Will he state what additional powers we could give them to afford them that status?

I have not the
statute before me and am not able to argue with the closeness I should desire	to	do. I	only heard the
statute read by the Minister of Justice. But this tribunal is not a court established under section 101 of the British

North America Act . and has not the full powers with regard to the taking of evidence of the country which a court established under that section would have. All the hon. gentleman needs to do is to create by statute a court under section 101 of the British North America Act. Ample power is given. Let the court be endo'wed with the same power that is given to the Supreme Court of Judicature of every province of the Dominion. Then you will have a body which will have the right to send commissioners to a foreign country to take evidence there. You will then have a court, and you will have a proceeding before that court, which are the essentials of the statute of the state of New York to which reference has been made. But now you have neither a court nor a proceeding' before a court, and consequently you have not a tribunal which can issue a commission to a foreign country and there command respect.
It has been disclosed before this com-misslion thalt the Governmenrt's position in regard to the Shell Committee as taken in this House is absolutely incorrect. It has been shown that this Shell Committee were not the agents of the British Government but were contractors appointed by the Minister of Militia of the Dominion of Canada to enter into a contract under which action could be brought against them individually. Their position in that matter was such that they seriously consulted the Prime Minister as to their personal liability for debts they might contract. These facts have been disclosed before this tribunal for the first time. Yet Mr. Johnston, who is conducting cross-examination, is not allowed to go into the matters which are pertinent and necessary in order to get the full facts before the country. It is for this House and the country to understand that the Government refuse to permit an enlargement of the powers of the commission for thi6 purpose.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That this matter, or some similar matter, should come before the attention of Parliament at this time can be to none of us a matter of surprise. Those who have had the privilege of watching the proceedings before the Royal Commission whose name has often been mentioned in this discussion, and have also studied the strategy of certain hon. gentlemen opposite, could quite readily come to the conclusion that the time had about come when some

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
explanations of the course of events at that commission might well be sent out through the country on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite by way of excuse for what was transpiring, such explanations masquerading, of course, as grievances and complaints.
What actually is before the House, however, I find it very difficult to see. What the House is asked to do is a matter which, though the debate has proceeded for some length of time, and though we have heard from three hon. gentlemen opposite, we may well say we do not know as yet. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), came to the House yesterday, and again to-day, with a motion that this House adjourn in order that he might discuss " a definite matter of urgent public importance," that definite matter of urgent public importance being as follows:
The desirability in the public interest of immediately enlarging the powers of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the contracts regarding fuses, etc., called the Meredith-Duff Commission, by providing for widening the scope of the inquiry into the matters referred to the Commission.
We are asked to discuss, to put it briefly, the desirability of widening the scope of the inquiry into the matters referred to the commission. We are not asked to refer any other matters to the commission. So far as the motion before the House goes, there is no suggestion that the scope of the commission as regards the matters before it is not wide enough. We are asked to consider the desirability of widening the scope of the inquiry into the matters referred to the commission. If the hon. member for Carleton really knew what he wanted-

I will save my hon.
friend some difficulty when I tell him that I did not prepare that at all. The note which I handed to the Speaker yesterday asked for an enlargement of the scope of the inquiry. When I came to my place to-day the motion in its present form was sent to me from the Speaker's Chair; I accepted it and read it. I am not going to split hairs about what is in it or what is not in it; that is the way it happened. Please forget that and we will get along.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not one of those, Mr. Speaker, who can forget what we are discussing when I am doing the discussing. I need to have something before me to be discussed. I must commend the discretion
of the hon. member for Carleton in renouncing the authorship of this resolution, although I think that the renunciation would have been" more becoming had it come earlier in the discussion. But how can a man renounce what he moves the House ot adopt? Notwithstanding the fact that he absolves himself from the responsibility, there is nothing before us 'for discussion except this. I do not know what there is to talk about unless it is what is before us: the desirability of widening the scope of the inquiry into the matters referred to the commission. If hon. gentlemen knew how the scope of the inquiry into the matters referred to the commission could be widened, they would have said so; the hon. member for Carleton would have come to this House with a definite statement of how the scope of that inquiry into those matters could be widened, and he would have asked the House to grant such added powers. I say to him now that if he can still come with any definite, understandable statement or resolution widening the scope of the inquiry into the matters .before that commission, it will get sympathetic consideration on the part of this Government. We thought we had given the scope the utmost wideness that the English language could give it in the Order in Council under which the commission now exists and is acting.
The course of the discussion has rambled from one thing to another. From their language, some hon. gentlemen would appear to desire that the commission be empowered to inquire into other subjects altogether. I think that actually is the desire oif hon. gentlemen opposite, though it takes the guise of this rather meaningless resolution. Others argue that what they are bringing before the House is a complaint as to the soundness of a view of law entertained by the members of the commission. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) and the hon. member for St. John city (Mr. Pugsley) assert that a decision on a point of law has been given that would be known to be wrong by any ordinary lawyer, and they ask the House of Commons of Canada to sit as a court of appeal from the judgments in law of the Chief Justice of Ontario and of Mr. Justice Duff of the Supreme Court. That is the second proposal made by hon. gentlemen opposite. Let us consider the first. They want us to widen the scope of the inquiry into these matters. The language of the commission says that everything relating to the four contracts may
34%

be inquired into: everything relating to the relation, if any, of the Minister of Militia to them; everything relating to the relations with them, if any, of any one else directly or indirectly associated with the Government or the Shell Committee; anything relating to the subcontracting under those contracts; all things relating to the profits arising or accruing directly or indirectly under the contracts, and to whom they accrue. The powers of the commission in that regard have been acknowledged as ample by the members of the commission themselves. They have been stated in the widest possible language by the counsel for the commission, Mr. Hell-muth. More than that, they have been stated as complete by Mr. Johnston, named by the leader of the Opposition. This gentleman admits-and admits more than once in the course of the very quotation read by the hon. member for Carleton, N.B.- that in relation to the four contracts, the matters referred to the commission, he has every possible liberty, and asks for no more. Why, then, should this House inquire into, the advisability of extending what already they admit is ample and complete?
Ai word more as to the second interpretation. It is said by two hon. members opposite: "We have not been treated fairly; Sir William Ralph Meredith has given a decision that is entirely unfair to us, and we want this House to review it. In the first place, even if there were any doubt as to its soundness, I must question the capacity of the House of Commons of Canada to sit in review over a commission of judges on a decision of law. In the next place, the very hon. gentleman who brings this resolution before the House admits that the decision is correct and that he has no fault to find with it. He admitted that yesterday, and he repeats his admission in still more emphatic language to-day. Here are his words:
I wish here in the most emphatic manner to state that I do not wish to he considered as casting any reflections whatever upon the decision of the commissioners.
These are the words of the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., who moves this resolution; so that it is not his desire to call in question, the fairness of the treatment accorded hon. gentlemen opposite before that commission. Where then does the hon. member for Pictou stand, and the hon. member for St. John, when we compare their language and their accusations with

the words of the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., who brings the matter before the House? So that so far as these two suggestions of what it is we are asked to consider are concerned, hon. gentlemen have answered themselves so clearly and so manifestly that further discussion is superfluous.
May I at this point of the discussion, say that I feel no surprise that hon. gentlemen opposite find it impossible to explain what they want in language, which, while coherent, does not at once expose its own absurdity? The counsel who is acting for them-at all events acting for the commission but named by them-himself found it impossible to state to the commission in understandable terms what he wanted and what he complained of. As soon as he finished, the Chief Justice said, " Why, that amounts to inquiring generally into all that the Shell Committee did." So that the decision of the justices is this:	"You ask
us to inquire into the details of certain contracts that have no relation at all to these four contracts under inquiry, and you say you want it because you want to get at the status of the committee. " They say:	"There is plenty before the
court to get at that status already'; what you want to do is, under cover of inquiring into the status of the committee, to divert the inquiry from what we are here to inquire into and turn it away and scatter it' off until it is lost in a wilderness where there are no charges to be found at all." That is substantially the answer which this disingenuous proposition received at the hands of the commission.
It was very plainly intimated yesterday by the hon. member for Carleton that this request had the endorsation of the justices. Here is what he said:
Mr. Johnston rather persisted in the matter, and finally the commission made the statement that it might he advisable to apply to Parliament in order that further powers might he given to them.
The impression any one would get from that was that the commission were of opinion that their powers should be extended, and suggested that application be made to Parliament to that end. I did not think that was the case, and took occasion to inquire more definitely; and the second answer of the hon. member for Carleton was, I think, fairly in accord with what the commission did say.
But the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) comes in and says this very

thing is the suggestion of the commissioners themselves; they make, he says, the suggestion to Parliament that this be done. Have they done so? Have the commissioners made the suggestion to Parliament that their powers be extended in that way? Does any hon. member say that they have done so? The commissioners * said: "If you want our powers extended, Parliament is the forum; this is not the forum; if you want it, go there and ask for it." It might be said that the commission suggested to them: " Go and ask for it." That suggestion has been fulfilled. But, so far from suggesting that it be granted, the commissioners very clearly discouraged any such idea. Here is what Sir William Meredith said, at page 374:
You have not made at all clear to me the scope of the inquiry you desire to enter into.
I quite agree with him.
Do you propose to enter upon an inquiry as to contracts, the details of contracts that were entered into with regard to other matters than the four that are referred to this commission to examine into the prices at which those contracts were let or taken from the War Office, and the prices at which they were let to those who contracted with the Shell Committee-is that what you propose to do?
I am afraid I have not the right quotation; but, as that one is somewhat pertinent, I do not regret having read it. I quote from page 376:
You are aware, of course, the Order in Council provides for the reference of other questions to this commission if it is thought expedient to do so. If anybody thinks that these matters ought to be inquired into, and we are to stay here all summer doing it, I suppose representation can be made-Mr. Carvell is a member of the House, he can bring the matter up and ask that the power of the inquiry be extended, but we must keep within the terms of our map.
Any suggestion that Parliament ehould grant the request, or should seriously consider such a suggestion as this? Clearly a discouragement of the idea in so far as the commission felt justified in going. I have disposed of all I can find in the way of a suggestion by the commission to the hon. gentlemen opposite.
Apparently under cover of this application the hon. gentlemen propose to escape, if they can, from the position in which they find themselves at this moment. Instead of having their exact position, humiliating as it may be becoming, go to the country in its true form, they make this rather ungraceful attempt to hide themselves behind the dust of a purely artificial grievance.
They say to us also: " Why do you not make this a court? Why do you not erect
this to the status of a court under section 191 of the British North America Act? If you do that, then it will have the power to issue a commission down in the United States, and that commission can summon witnesses there." What is the purpose of a suggestion like that? The purpose of that is one thing and one only: it is to have it go out to the country, if they can manage it, that there is somebody whom they want but cannot get. Who is he? Has his name appeared? We did hear names mentioned not long ago of men who, it was asserted, would not appear; but they are here. Who is this man in New York whom they have endeavoured, without success, to get, under their present powers. There is nobody, so far as I have been able to hear. We are told to erect this commission to the status of a court: a Commission of Inquiry under the Inquiries Act is not high enough. What did hon. gentlemen opposite want three weeks ago? They wanted a committee of Parliament. Would it have had the status of a court under section 191 of the British North America Act? It would have had no such status but would have had a history that would have done no credit to Parliament, if we may judge from these proceedings this afternoon. What would have been the character and volume of the complaints that would have been hurled at the doors of Parliament day after day if the decisions of a member of this House as chairman had to be taken, on a matter of law, instead of the decisions of the Chief Justice of Ontario?
They now want us to give this commission the status of a court, and they say: " If you will do that, there is a law down in New York which says that whenever there is a court in another country that has powers in relation to civil and criminal proceedings, that court may issue a commission, and if that commission sits in the State of New York witnesses may be compelled to attend." Now, they say, call this a court to-day, and put a clause in to say that this Commission of Inquiry under the Inquiries Act shall have all the status and powers of a	court	under
section 191 of the British North America Act. We have plenary powers to put that in the statute. The question comes, what will be its effect after it is put in? If its effect is anything, it will be just the same as if we were to insert: "This commission shall be considered a court by the state of New York." That is another way of legis-

lating for the state of New York. Let tne give an illustration. A town council, within the limits of its powers, has a certain power of inquiry delegated to it by the provincial authorities, whose posters are as plenary as ours. The town council appoints a committee of inqiiiry into some question in a certain ward. How would it be for that town council to solemnly enact that this committee shall have all the powers of a court under section 191 of the British North America Act, and must be so recognized by the law of the state of New York? Would it not follow that the committee would immediately be entitled to that recognition if the argument of the hon. member for St. John is correct?
A court is a court, by virtue of its functions, not by virtue of its name; and you cannot make a committee a court or a commission a court acting under a statute that authorizes inquiry simply by calling it a court. However, it will be time enough to consider this when a case arises, and I say here and now that w'hen hon. gentlemen come to this House and state that they have witnesses down in New York or in New Jersey-the hon. member for Pictou wants to discuss the laws of the state of New Jersey too-if they have a witness hiding in New York or New Jersey, and come before Parliament and say so and that they desire to get him and cannot, and bring to Parliament some means that will enable Parliament to procure his evidence, this Government will do everything in its power to meet their request to the full. All that hon. gentlemen have to do is to bring before us some means that will be effective, and if there is any means dv which it can be effected we will effect it.
I have covered the only four possible meanings there' can be to this remarkable (notion. In such form the request of the hon. gentlemen is manifestly absurd It was so denominated by the Chief Commissioner, so denominated by the counsel for the commission, Mr. Hellmuth, and so denominated by counsel acting for themselves. If they are asking us to sit in review upon a judgment in law of Chief Justice Meredith, I do not think Parliament will do itself any honour by acceding to that request. There are certain functions that, others can exercise even better than we can. Besides if they are attacking that decision on the ground that it is wrong, we have the authority of the mover of the motion himself for saying that the decision is right. If they are asking for an extension of the

scope of inquiry for a reference of other matters, or if they have intended to do so-for they have not done it-then I agree with the commissioners that all they want is to divert the course of the inquiry now proceeding in a defined field where charges of a certain attenuated character have been made and turn it into a field where there are no charges at all in order that its whole force may be dissipated and lost. If, on the other hand, they want the powers extended to get witnesses, if we have any means that will extend them, and if there are any witnesses who are not here already and will not come, we will adopt effective powers that mqy be suggested to us that will assist to bring such witnesses before this tribunal.

Mr. Speaker, I am satisfied that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister appreciates the position which I take, and I must say that he handled it fairly and frankly and in a perfectly intelligent and logical manner, as he always does when discussing questions before this House. The position is simply this: We realize that the scope of the commission, in its ordinary acceptance, refers to the investigation of fouT contracts. During the investigation, as I have tried to make perfectly plain, from the evidence matters have developed that in our judgment have placed us at a great disadvantage. Statements have been made as to the alleged savings of the Shell Committee which we were not allowed to investigate, and a new position of affairs has been created, in view of the fact that the members of the Shell Committee are legally acting in a contractual relationship with this Government, or with the Minister of Militia as the representative of this Government. Therefore we consider that conditions have so changed that, acting on the suggestion of Chief Justice Meredith, we have come here, and I have presented the facts to this House as fairly, as truthfully, and as logically as I know how to present them.
I do not think I am called on to say much in reply to what has been advanced by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. I do not find much fault with the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), nor would I expect much else from him. I have tried to treat the House with absolute fairness and to state the facts as they are. I was somewhat pained that the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) should have so far frogotten himself to talk of the politi-

cal side of this question rather than the legal side of it.
Some hon. MEMBEKS: Oh, oh.

My hon. friends may
say, "oh, oh," but I can assure them that I am not going to be drawn into that side of it no matter what the Minister of Justice may have said. I say that I was sorry that he should have suggested that we were running away from the position. I tried tp discuss this question purely as a legal matter, and perhaps, if I retorted to my hon. friend from Dufferin (Mr. Best) a little severely it was because I did not want to be drawn away from that phase of the question-

People know now that you
are trying to get away from it.

-and I thought nobody else would treat the matter in a different way from that. I was discussing the matter purely with reference to the legal end of it. I would, however, digress to the extent of reminding my hon. friend that this matter is not being tried in an ordinary court, or in the way in which matters are tried in an ordinary court.. In this case the defendant is putting in his defence first, and he has got about half way through with it. Therefore I would ask my hon. friend, before he passes final adjustment on this matter, to wait until the plaintiff, if there be such a person, or a person occupying that position, has had his turn. Then it will be time enough for the Minister of Justice to talk about running away from the position. I have nothing further to say upon that.
I hope the Solicitor General will pardon me if I do not travel over his somewhat technical discussion, because unfortunately I was compelled to take away from him the main ground of his argument by stating that the wording of the resolution was not mine. I adopted that which had been sent to me by Mr. Speaker. Of course, the Speaker's mind is broad enough to realize that we are discussing an important principle. I am not surprised that the Solicitor General attempted to get some comfort out of the actual wording of the resolution. As far as I recollect, and I have not been able to attend all the sittings of the House during the last ten days, I think the Solicitor General has had the first opportunity of exercising that fine talent for distinguishing the difference between tweedledee and
tweedledum that his mind is so admirably fitted for since he was placed in a rather unfortunate position by my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) about a month ago. Therefore it is not to be wondered at that he should seize the opportunity to rehabilitate himself amongst his friends. As to how he has succeeded I have no comment to offer. I hope he will pardon me if I do not make any further reference to his argument, because it was of such a hairsplitting character that I could not understand him and I am sure that nobody else could. I am satisfied that I have presented this matter in good faith, I am sincere about it, and I believe that the scope of the inquiry can be broadened so as to go into the matters to which I have referred. I do believe, notwithstanding the arguments of the Minister of Justice-and I always like to listen to him, because he tries to elucidate matters-that the Inquiries Act should be so amended as to give us the right to get evidence in the United States if it turns out that such a thing may be necessary. For these reasons I hope that the suggestion which I made will be adopted by the House.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. J. D. Reid (Acting Minister of Railways), Bill No. 96, to aid in the construction of certain lines of railway of the St. John and Quebec Railway Company, and to confirm an agreement between the company and the Governments of Canada and New Brunswick, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.
On section 1-short title:

maintopic: THE ST. JOHN AND QUEBEC RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I have already expressed my views with regard to what seems to be the unsatisfactory nature of the agreement which has finally been arrived at and which makes this Valley railway have one of its termini at Andover, a station of the Canadian Pacific railway, and the other at Westfield, another station of the Canadian Pacific railway. Having expressed my

views, I will not weary the House by repeating what I said upon, a former occasion. I would like, however, to point out to my hon. friend the Acting' Minister of Railways that the agreement provides that the running rights which may be obtained by the company shall be subject to the approval of the Governor in Council- I would suggest that it would be desirable to make those running rights also subject to the approval of the Lieutenant Governor in Council of the province of New Brunswick. It would be very unfortunate if the company or this Government were not able to make a satisfactory arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the St. John Bridge and Railway Extension Company for running rights between Westfield and St. John. If they were not able to make such satisfactory arrangement passengers would have to change cars at Westfield and other inconveniences would arise. There should be provision for trains of the Government having running rights into the city of St. John to the station upon the eastern side and also for the Government freight trains to have running rights to their destination upon either side of the haTbour. There has been passed at the present	session a Railway Act, a
very excellent Act in some respects and the provision which gives the Board of Railway Commissioners power, in order to prevent the paralleling of lines of railway, to order the owners of an existing railway to give running rights to another company whose railway is under construction, is an exceedingly good one; but, as the St. John and Quebec Railway Company is a company incorporated by the Legislature of New Brunswick, I would not think that the Board of Railway Commissioners would have power to order, either the Canadian Pacific Raiilway Company or the St. John Bridge and Railway Extension Company to grant running righte to that company, and therefore it would have to be a matter of arrangement. The difficulty could be gotten over if the minister would consent to place in the Bill a section declaring the undertaking of the St. John and Quebec Railway Company to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. That would bring the road under the operation of the Railway Act and would give the Board of Railway Commissioners power to make the necessary arrangements for running rights. I am sure that the minister will see thait that would be desirable, and I think he will also agree with me that 221
a railway which is to be leased to the Government of Canada and operated as a part of the Intercolonial Railway system should be subject to the jurisdiction of that body, and that even upon that ground, if the other very important reason which I suggested did not exist, it would be desirable to declare the undertaking to be a work for the general advantage of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
maintopic: THE ST. JOHN AND QUEBEC RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The hon. member mentioned those matters in the discussion the other evening. In regard to the running rights between Westfield and St. John, the Bill provides that the company shall acquire the running rights from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; but in the event of their failure to make a satisfactory arrangement that may be necessary, the Dominion Government will make the arrangement that may be necessary to operate the trains between Westfield and St. John. It ds quite true that if the company were not able to make an arrangement themselves, the position would be a difficult one; but as the Dominion Government are to operate this road, they would have power, by making application to the Board of Railway Commissioners, to have that Board act in so far as the operation on behalf of the Dominion Government is concerned. I would have no objection at all to having this work declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. The only difficulty that I am in this evening is that I feel that any changes that we might make in connection with this agreement might not be in accordance with the wishes of the Provincial Gqvernment, who of course are the owners of the road. If the Bill as it stands covers all the points raised by the hon. member for St. John I should prefer to have it go through in that way. As I stated the other evening, the arrangements were satisfactory to i,hi Provincial Government, and I have rn>
doubt whatever that a satisfactory arrangement can be made with the Canadian Pacific for running rights over that portion of their road into St. John. But, as I stated, if the Dominion Government do not consider the running arrangements satisfactory they can provide a line of their own into St. John. The hon. member raised the point that arrangements should be satisfactory to the Provincial Government. The Bill provides that the company has to make the arrangement. But the company is really the Provincial Government; they name the directors by Order in Council, and can put them



in or put them out. In addition, they have really taken over the road, as I understand it. Everything in that way is working harmoniously. We discussed the several matters in connection with the running rights, and neither party anticipated any great trouble in getting in from Westfield to St. John. But, as I have stated, I should 'have no objection to putting in the clause suggested by the hon. gentleman if I were quite sure it did not affect the Bill as a whole. Of course, he is aware that this agreement has been passed and is now law, so far as the New Brunswick Government is concerned. What I fear is that any changes made here might affect the law as passed in New Brunswick,- Perhaps we could let the Bill'go on and discuss that a little later.

maintopic: THE ST. JOHN AND QUEBEC RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The remarks the hon, minister has just made would apply to an alteration in the agreement, but I do not think they would apply to the clause in the Act declaring the work to be one for the general advantage of Canada. However, I do not wish to press it if the minister thinks he would like to put that clause off in order .to consult the Provincial Government. The road will probably not be finished before another session of Parliament, and if any question arises about getting running rights additional legislation can be passed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE ST. JOHN AND QUEBEC RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The principle
adopted, though under somewhat different condition, two or three years ago, was that Parliament delayed any declaration until after the work was completed. There is disadvantage in declaring a work to be one for the general advantage of Canada while it is still in course of construction. The reasons are so obvious that I do not need to point them out.

Is it the opinon of the
Militia Department, mow that we have had almost two years of war, that this service is of any real value? In times of peace it seems to me to be a waste of money to make this expenditure on the training of young boys, many of whom when they grow up will not join the volunteer force. It may, perhaps, be of some advantage during the war. I should like to have the view of the Prime Minister on this point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand that it is the view of the department that the service which is rendered by this vote is a very important one. The boys throughout the country do take a keen interest in it, and the training is of advantage not only to the country but to the boys themselves. They are taught habits of discipline and they receive certain military training at a time when what they do learn will remain with them always. The hon. gentleman doubts whether they are likely to continue their training in the militia force as they grow older. I am informed that the experience of the department, so far as they have had any experiece, is precisely the reverse; that the boys who receive training of this kind naturally take an interest in continuing their training as they grow older.

Some years ago when this question came before the House I was rather critical: if I did not oppose the item, I criticised it. Since that time, however, I have learned to know better. I am not a militarist, and I do not approve the movement because of any belief that it would promote militarism in Canada; but I believe that the principles upon which this movement is based in Canada, in England, and in France, which has copied it from England, are most excellent. I have seen these young men in Montreal and in Ottawa doing excellent service, and from what I have read I understand that in France, at the front, and at the rear of the armies, the cadets have been most useful as helpers in hospital work and in other work connected with the management of these large armies. I vote for this item with pleasure, for I believe that the movement is a healthy one in time of war or in time of peace. It teaches the young men to be manly.

Although these Estimates do not bear directly upon the war expenditure and administration, would the Prime Minister consider it to be in order to deal with such matters under these items if in the course of the discussion it should become desirable to secure information with regard to the administration of war affairs?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not any objection, if my hon. friend thinks that would be more convenient than to take it on the Bill when it comes up in committee.

The work is all carried on by the Militia Department, and neces-
221i
sarily it interlocks to a certain extent. If satisfactory to the Prime Minister, it might be just as convenient for the committee to deal with these matters now as at some future time. In regard to this vote for cadet services, I would like to offer this for the consideration of the committee and the Government. When there was no war, it was desirable that we should prepare for war, but now that we have war, it is desirable that we should meet that condition as promptly and efficiently as	possible. I have nothing but
praise for the idea of the training of young men for military service. But at the present time we have need, not so much of boys who will be of service some years from now, as of men who will be of service in case of emergency to-day. There are many men throughout the country who are willing and anxious to be enrolled for local service, as a military protection either as enrolled active militia or in corps similar to the cadets. There seems to be no disposition to encourage such a movement as this. These organizations get no pay, no arms, no uniforms, no consideration whatever, except the privilege of enrollment and of drilling without arms. This condition may be due to the stress of circumstances; but while the country is in this condition of war, while we hope that there may be no danger of complications of any kind arising in this country, at the same time it would be well to encourage such organizations for home defence or for military service in Canada. If we are not doing that because we have not the money, I would suggest that we would better spend this money on adults who are ready for service than on the boys, who no doubt are good boys, but who will not be ready for service until a number of years have passed.

I am surprised to find
that the conditions in the Northwest are different from what they are in the part of the country from which I come. The hon. gentleman has just made a plea in which he characterizes the Government's inactivity, in terms that are not very complimentary, with regard to those men who would like to join units that are not intended for overseas service. He says they do not receive good treatment when they make application to the department, that no consideration is given to them, that they have no uniforms and no rifles. Why, that is true in the case of the forces that

are going overseas. This country is pressed to the utmost limit to provide uniforms and rifles and equipment for those who are going to fight, and how the hon. gentleman can attack the Militia Department and the Government for not having this equipment for men who are not going to fight, passes all comprehension. In the neighbourhood in which I live, and I think this is generally true in western Ontario, the men who may desire to enlist for home defence are spending not only their business time but every spare moment of time in recruiting for overseas forces, going from town to town all over the district, holding meetings, urging the younger men fit for fighting service to come in and join the colours. Thus where I live the usefulness of the peace battalions has practically ceased. Officers fit for service who were in command have practically left their commands and gone into the fighting forces. So that the regimental units have been practically wiped out of existence, and practically all the men who are fit for service have gone or are going overseas to fight. The condition of which my hon. friend speaks is therefore a natural condition, and I am surprised to learn that the conditions are not the same in the West as they are with us.
As to abandoning the support of the cadet movement in favour of a movement such as the hon. gentleman has foreshadowed, or advocated, that it seems to me would be a great mistake, because the only home force to-day in western Ontario that is organized, that is available, is the cadet force, which is officered by regular officers attached to the schools of which the corps form a component part. They are composed of youths from 14 to 16 or 17 years of age. If there is any force that should be equipped for home defence, a force of energy, activity and intelligence, it is the cadet force. The hon. gentleman suggests that we substitute for them a non-existent section of the community.
Hundreds and thousands of these cadets have enrolled in the overseas forces and gone to the front not only with training but with intelligence and efficiency. Anything that would detract from, or cause deterioration in, the cadet forces would he the next thing to a national crime. I hope the committee will take the remarks I have made in the spirit in which they are offered. Whatever may be the conditions in other places, I would oppose any suggestion that would detract from the
fMr. Morphy.]
efficiency which is now being developed through the cadet movement, and which is reflected in the fighting forces of this country. I think it is the best movement that has taken place in the history of Canada.

I agree very largely with the remarks of my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) in regard to the Home Guard. In one of the towns in my constituency, when the war first started, a Home Guard was formed and a lot of our young men joined it. In the early part of last summer I was in that town attending a meeting for the purpose of helping recruiting, and they reorganized their Home Guard. Out of the first hundred members who joined the Home Guard when the war broke out 80 had joined the regular forces and were either across the water serving at the front with the First Contingent or had been drafted into various battalions that were being organized. They reorganized the Home Guard and some 150 more men joined it. Their complaint was that they could not get any help as to officers for drilling or rifles from the Militia Department. They particularly asked for rifles. There were some old Ross rifles that were not supposed to be first-class that had been sent out for the Border Horse. The Home Guard applied for these rifles. I had some correspondence over it with the Militia Department, and I asked them to communicate directly with the parties out there; therefore I am not prepared to say whether they eventually got any help or not from the Militia Department. I know there has been a shortage of rifles. Possibly the acting minister could say how many Canada can produce in the arsenal at Quebec. Are 'we producing a large number?.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know that it would be very prudent for me to give statistics- in regard to that. I may, however, -say that according to my information the Ross rifle factory has produced more rifles since the commencement of this war than any other establishment on this continent up to the present time. I am pretty sure, although not absolutely positive, that it is producing more to-day than any other establishment on this continent. I do not believe that will always continue, because very great preparations have been made in some of the establishments on the other side of the line; but I think I am quite within the limit when I make the statement to which I have just given ut-

terance. Might I say that while that is true, we really have not had any such supply of rifles as would enable us to meet the suggestion which the hon. member for Edmonton has thrown out. There is a certain amount of difficulty in providing uniforms and other articles of equipment for the men as fast as they are enlisted. The greatest difficulty of all is with the rifles. It is not a question of money, as my hon. friend from Edmonton seems to suggest, but it is a question of rifles. If he will tell us where we can get rifles, there is money enough on hand to purchase them; but we do not know where they can be secured except in the factory that we have at Quebec, and that has done fairly well. I appreciate very thoroughly the spirit of the mep who enlisted in the home guards in the early months of the war. I had the privilege of reviewing a great many regiments of home guards in different phrts of the country. There were men of all ages, old and young-young men, men in the prime of life, men getting on in years, fifty or sixty years of age and perhaps more. They were all drilling away, endeavouring so to train themselves as to do good service in case there were any call for it. As has been observed by my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), a great many of the younger of these men have since enlisted for overseas service in all parts of the country. The movement became so pronounced in various parts of the country that my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes) concluded that the better course for him would be to organize the reserve militia, which the Governor General had power to do, if I remember the provisions of the Militia Act correctly. An Order in Council was passed for that purpose. A good many units of the reserve militia have been organized in different parts of Canada. It is suggested that the Government give these no consideration. The Government give them all the consideration that is possible consistently with providing for the needs of the men who have enlisted for overseas service, and I feel sure that all will agree that that is the need which must first be provided for; so we have provided for that first. In some cases a few rifles have been procured for training of the battalions of the reserve militia, not very many, I am sorry to say, because they were urgently needed for other purposes which were regarded as of prior importance. Subject to those considerations, I am informed by the deputy minister that the department has been disposed to give, and does give, to these units of reserve militia all the consideration that is possible.

I quite agree with the Prime Minister that if rifles are short the men who are overseas naturally have to be attended to before the home guards, cadets or anybody else; but I understand that the Department of Militia, or the Government, sold a large number of old Lee-Enfield rifles prioT to the breaking out of the war.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am informed by the officers of the department that no rifles have been sold since the outbreak of the war. Some time before the war a small number of old rifles were sold through the British Government to the New Zealand Government.

Of course, I am aware
that those rifles were sold before August, 1914; but even before the war broke out rifle associations had a good deal of trouble in getting rifles. With regard to the Lee-Enfields, my information is that 15,000 of them were sold to the New Zealand Government at $1 apiece, and that the New Zealand troops in Flanders and France and other war zones are now using those very rifles.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Where did my hon. friend get that information?

I could give my right
hon. friend my authority for it. If my information is not correct, the officers of the department who are here to-night can set me right. I know these rifles were sold to the New Zealand Government, because they are mentioned in the Auditor General's Report, and the New Zealand Government put a certain amount to the credit of the Canadian Government in London in payment for them. I had a letter from one of our soldiers in the trenches not
9 p.m. long ago, and he said that the Ross rifle, with which they were armed, was not considered as good a rifle as the Lee-Enfield, and that whenever our soldiers had the opportunity of picking up a Lee-Enfield, they threw the Ross rifle away. If that is true we have the anomaly of the Canadian soldier throwing away a rifle which costs $17 or $18, or $27 or $28-I am not sure which, but it is a considerable sum anyway-and picking up a rifle which our own Government sold to the New Zealand

Government for $1. I know exactly where this letter came from, and can depend on the writer when he says our soldiers are throwing away the Boss and picking up the Lee-Enfield.

Are the New Zealand
forces armed with the Lee-Enfields that my hon. friend has just referred to?

That is my information.
Mr. MOEPHY': On what date were those rifles sold by the Canadian Government?

I do not know whether it was in 1912 or 1913, but they were sold by this Government some time before the war began. I could not prove that these'' rifles the Government sold are now being used by the New Zealand soldiers at the front, but the Auditor General's report shows that they were sold to the New Zealand Government at all events.

I have heard stories of our men picking up the Lee-Enfield rifle, and I have ako heard stories of British soldiers picking up the Boss rifle in preference to their own. I have been told it is not an uncommon thing for a soldier, when a rifle of a different type is available, to think for the time being it is better than his own, and to favour the idea of making the change. As far as the sale of rifles is concerned, I should like my hon. friend to bear in mind that the Boss rifle was adopted by the late Administration, instead of the Lee-Enfield, as the rifle our soldiers were to be armed with. It was a model weapon that was adopted. It is perfectly true that the contract made by the late Administration with the Boss Bifle Company provided that the Government might from time to time require the production of rifles of a different model, if it saw fit, provided it would pay the cost of the neo ssary machinery, gauges and other alterations of a complex character that the change would necessitate. The Lee-Enfield rifles, ,and some of the Lee-Metfords, I think, were disposed of, as they were not required while that policy was being carried on. The policy with regard to the Boss rifle was not changed when the present Administration came into power. I deprecate the idea of endeavouring to convey * the impression, either to the House or to the country, but especially to our own troops, that the rifle with which they are armed is not a suitable weapon. Any idea of that kind, I think, would be most un-

fortunate, and do a great deal of 'harm. If we had any choice a3 to the rifle to be used there might be some obiect in it, but inasmuch as, under present conditions, we have to use the Boss rifle or nothing, I for one can see no good reason why any hon. gentleman in this House should seek to cast discredit on the rifle with which our troops are armed. There was a good deal of discussion about the Boss rifle some years ago, and there ha3 been some discussion since the war broke out. To avoid a particular difficulty that occurred at the front a change has been made in the Boss rifle. A difficulty occurred at the front, not only with the Boss rifle, but with the Lee-Enfield as well, and a change corresponding to that made in the Boss rifle has also been made, I am informed, in the Lee-Enfield, and with good results in both cases.
The ammunition caused the guns to jam, I think.

The change that was made was an enlargement of the chamber. The chamber of the Boss rifle, I understand, was slightly smaller than that of the Lee-Enfield. The Lee-Enfield chamber was slightly enlarged, and the chamber of the Boss rifle enlarged to a still greater extent, and I believe that the enlarged chamber of the Boss rifle is now somewhat larger than the enlarged chamber of the Lee-Enfield. It is said, however, by those who are in a better position to judge of these matters than I am, that the jamming to which allusion has been made was occasioned by the character of a certain quality of amunition which at one time was being served out, but which I think has since been withdrawn. I am informed that neither with the Boss nor the Lee-Enfield has any great difficulty been experienced when other ammunition was used. As a matter of fact, when our own ammunition, manufactured in this country, was used in the Boss rifle no considerable difficulty in jamming occured.

I saw it stated
in the newspapers quite recently in regard to the heavy fighting that took place within the last two weeks at St. Eloi and other places that some jamming occurred. Whether it was the fault of the ammunition or whether those things occur under the best * conditions or not I do not know, but I saw criticisms of that kind in the Montreal Gazette and other leading Canadian newspapers.
\

I am a little inclined
to doubt the accuracy of the information of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) in regard to the old Lee-Enfield rifles sold to New Zealand being used by the soldiers at the front. I have a very distinct recollection, when the Liberal Government was in power, of that Government handing around hundreds of those rifles throughout the country wherever any number of young men formed a rifle association. The Government would provide them with the rifles free of cost, and also with all the old ammunition which the Government were discarding and which those young men saw fit to use. I belong to one of those associations, and my recollection of that rifle is that when you fire it off it will pretty nearly kick you into the next county. While I think the Government did a proper thing in discarding those old rifles and giving out the old ammunition, thereby encouraging rifle associations, I cannot think that those rifles would be used in actual warfare, although for a person who had his shoulder well padded they might do all right to use in firing at a target.
Why would the New Zealand Government buy such a large quantity as 15,000?

They might use those
rifles for drilling purposes or for target practice. If a person had a bag filled with sawdust up against his shoulder, and if he placed his feet very firmly on the ground, he might remain in the county in which he was when he fired off his rifle. I do not think, however, from all I can hear, that troops like those supplied by New Zealand would use a rifle that was not up to date, and I do not think the New Zealand Government would place in the hands of their men a rifle that was purchased at a dollar apiece. I think the hon. member is drawing largely on a very excellent and active imagination when he supposes anything of that kind.

The discussion
has rather switched from what we had in mind when this item was first called, and, if I might be permitted, I would like to take this opportunity of threshing out this question of policy in regard to arming and equipping and recognizing local forces throughout the Dominion. That question is an important one and one that is entirely pertinent to the subject under discussion. When we find it desirable to train
and measurably equip boys for the sake'of the service that they may'render in years to epme, and that is all very proper, we should not ignore the present need of men who can render service now, who are willing to render that service, but whom we are not willing to equip so as to enable them to render that service. There is, in parts of the Northwest, at any rate in Alberta, an organization called the' Legion of Frontiersmen, formed for the purpose of military drill. That legion was organized long before the war and had exactly the same purposes, if I understand the matter correctly, as the cadet corps, only it was composed of mature men, and possibly to some degree of elderly men, and not of boys. That legion has organizations at various points throughout the province of Alberta for the purpose of securing military efficiency in order to be able to render to the country a service which, while it was only in prospect when the war broke out, may at any moment become an imperative necessity now that war conditions exist. There is no question about the good faith of those men, nor about their loyalty of purpose, nor about the efforts that they have made in the sacrifice of time and energy in fitting themselves for military service by military drill; but military drill is only an empty thing unless it has the support of actual weapons. I know that this organization has applied repeatedly tc the Department of Militia for arms and for such recognition as is granted to the cadets, but I am informed that such recognition has been not only constantly refused, but refused with some abruptness that was perhaps not necessary under the circumstances. My contention is this, that when the country is at war, and when no man can forecast what contingency may arise, so long as we are dependent upon voluntaryism for our military service, it is the part of wisdom for the Government to encourage military organization under every possible circumstance that will measurably tend to efficiency and to good results, and that when the Government absolutely . ignores the offer of service on the part of those men who form this Legion of Frontiersmen, they discriminate against men who are able to render service to-day in favour of boys who can be expected to render service only some years hence. I do not think that is good policy; I do not think it is what the necessities of the country require at the present time. I have already spoken of the active militia being organized, tout not provided with weapons or with uni-

forms, being without pay or recognition, and only permitted to enroll themselves under the orders of the 'Government, and yet they may be called to any part of the Dominion at any time that	the
occasion may arise. The idea that is in the minds of those who are	not
prepared at the moment to enlist for overseas service, but who desire to render themselves efficient in a military sense by means of drill and organization, is that the men who enlist for overseas service will be sent . overseas and leave the country depleted of an active military force. It may not be the intention of the Government to send overseas the men who have enlisted for that service; their intention may be to keep in Canada a large proportion of those men.
If that is tfieir intention I can only say that I do not think they keep faith with the men who enlist. The man who gives up his business, gives up his prospects, believing that the country demands that sacrifice from him, will certainly not think that the country is doing fairly by him if, instead of giving him the opportunity to render the service that he has sacrificed in order to render, it keeps him doing drill and sentry-go in Canada around his own home. That is not his intention or desire, and if that is the intention of the Government in securing his enlistment, it is certainly not in conformity with the views and wishes of the men who enlist. The idea is that men who isnlist for overseas service shall be sent overseas, and that there shall be a local military organization sufficiently large and efficient, and well enough equipped, to protect the interests of the country at home. While that is the idea of the people, I take the liberty of criticising what appears to be the policy of the Militia Department, which, judging by their action, is to ignore everything except the enlistment for overseas service. The men who enlisted for overseas service being held in Canada for a longer time than they believe they ought to be held, are dissatisfied and do not recognize that they are being dealt with fairly by the Government. I say that in time of war, under a voluntary system such as we have and must depend upon, the policy should be to encourage military drill and military efficiency in every section of the population that is willin'! to take up that drill and secure that efficiency.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know that it will be of any use for me to repeat [Mr. Oliver.!
again what I have already said in terms as distinct as I can make them. We have not enough rifles to train the men who are going overseas. We regard the necessity in that respect as above the- necessity for the reserve militia referred to. The hon. gentleman says we ignore them because we do not give them rifles.
