I tell him again we have not the rifles to give them; all the rifles we have are required for the forces training for overseas. I cannot make the matter any plainer. If the hon. gentleman would like a statement of the exact number of rifles available and the exact number of men under training, I should be very glad to give it to him for his own information, and perhaps be would then understand the situation better then than he seems to do now. So far as the defence of Canada is concerned, I think it was stated a year ago last autumn, or last December, that under the policy which the Government proposed there would probably be at all times in Canada not less than 50,000 men under training, who would be available for the defence of the country in case of attack. There are certainly more than twice that number in training in Canada at present, and as regiments go forward new regiments are formed. The total enlistments up to the present time run to about 320,000. The enlistments from the first of January to the first of May-I have not the exact figures before' me-were between 112,000 and 115,000, or at the rate of nearly a thousand a day. The troops have been going overseas just as fast as the conditions permitted: first, the adequacy of there training here, so that they can complete that training in Great Britain; second, the arrangements made by the British Government for their reception in the British Islands while that further training is being carried on; and, third, the provision of transports to take them across the Atlantic. By all these conditions we have been limited. Perhaps there might be mentioned a fourth, which is the provision of equipment and rifles-though we have not always waited for rifles, but have- sometimes sent them, across without rifles which followed them safely afterwards.

I
desire first to express my appreciation of the splendid manner in which the Government is handling this stupendous problem of equipping men, training them, and sending them overseas. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the complete answer to the criticism of hon. gentlemen opposite, this

evening and at other times, is to be found in the fact that the records made by our troops who have gone overseas prove conclusively that the method used by the 'Government, the system under which these men are enrolled and trained, is a sound and good one. I do not think we could have a stronger testimony to the efficiency of the Government and of the Department of Militia than the record of our troops at the front.
There are one or two things I wish to draw to the attention of the Prime Minister. It has been brought to my attention that in the Motherland it is often very difficult to distinguish a Canadian soldier, because so many of them wear no distinct badge. On the contrary, New Zealanders and Australians wore badges that were 'quite distinct. I understand that the badge we use is a composition and that not all our soldiers wear a brass badge. The suggestion is made that we should have a common badge for all battalions which every 'Canadian soldier should wear, so that our men can be distinguished. That suggestion comes to me from a very prominent commander of a battalion at the front. Another point is this: of the men offering themselves for enlistment, probably from twenty to thirty per cent are rejected for some minor physical defect. A man may be an inch or two short in chest measurement, or he may have some defect in his teeth-though I understand that teeth defects are being remedied at the expense of the Government. Many of these minor defects for which men are rejected could he remedied by a brief course of physical training. It has been suggested to me, and I think the suggestion is worthy of consideration, that special instructors should be used to take men who are capable of being developed into suitable subjects for enlistment and give them a few weeks of special training. It is easy to see that if you can save five per cent of the men offering for enlistment it would add very materially to the forces going to the front. I know that there are men in different parts of Canada, well trained for this work and who could give special physical instruction to these recruits, and probably a few weeks would bring many of them up to efficiency.
Then, in giving commissions to officers taking troops overseas, I believe the policy should be followed at all times of bringing back from the front men who have seen service. We sent overseas in the first contingent a large number of bright, educated, clever men, highly capable of commanding
men or directing their activities in civil life, and who have proven themselves to be very efficient at the front.
I think that from now on the policy should be adopted as a definite and final one that all commissions shall be given to those men who have served at the front. I understand that the Government have already adopted t'he policy to a very large extent, and that many men are being brought back from the front who have seen active service. The whole question of commissions has become a very serious one in this country. Many men feel that they ought to have commissions, but while this is a proper and laudable ambition, it would be infinitely better if a man were compelled to have from three to six months' active service at the front before being allowed to take command of a body of men. Exception, of course, might be made in the case of those who have been in military life for many years and have undergone extensive training. I feel very strongly on the question of commissions and the type of men who should receive them. I wish to cast no reflection on men who hold commissions in Canada to-day, or in the training camps of England, but it appears to me that no one could criticise the policy of bringing non-commissioned officers and others recommended by their senior officers back from the front for that purpose. This applies particularly to commanding officers. I think it would be very desirable to bring back, say, majors or captains from the front and give them command of battalions in Canada. Knowing the entirely new and strange conditions under which the men now have to operate, they could impart very much better training than men who had not seen service at the front. I throw out these few suggestions for the consideration of the Government without wishing to add unnecessarily to their burdens, at the same time expressing my appreciation of the splendid manner in which this department has handled the gigantic task resting upon it. I can scarcely understand how the Prime Minister can carry the burden which is resting upon him, not only the responsibility of the Prime Minister's office, but also that of the Department of Militia. I think the committee should give to the Prime Minister every possible consideration in the matter of carrying out these very onerous duties.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Every Canadian who goes overseas has a badge

on his shoulder, , the word " Canada," and he has, as I understand, a regimental badge on his collar. The type of cap used is practically uniform with that used in the British Army. It is not eo distinctive as that used by the Australians and New Zealanders, who are more readily distinguished in that way. With regard to bringing back men from the front for the training of those in Canada, that has been done to a considerable extent. A great many of the unite which have been organized during the past six months have been eo organized by men who were brought back from the front. So far as commissions are concerned, I am informed by the deputy minister that the practice at the front is this: if, for example, a lieutenant is invalided, the next senior non-commissioned officer is promoted, and if the lieutenant does not return within thirty days to duty the position taken by the noncommissioned officer is made permanent. Promotions are made from the ranks to make good his place and that of the corporal and other non-commissioned officers; so that the department has been endeavouring to carry out that principal, giving preferment to -men who have served at the front for a certain time.
The badge is a composition badge, I understand. The information I have from a very reliable source is that it does not wear well, and the suggestion is that it should be a brass badge.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: A brass badge can be seen at a considerable distance and is very conspicuous. It is all very well in the streets of ILondbn, but not so -appropriate at the front; and for that reason the composition badge is used instead.

The idea which the h-on. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) puts forth is a very laudable one. I agree with the Prime Minister as to the difficulty of obtaining the necessary rifles for the equipping of the home forces -along the lines suggested! The problem of obtaining sufficient arms to equip the troops is one that I am sure is very serious. I understand that the difficulty of obtaining -arms on this side of the water is taxing the capacity of every factory; especially do we realize this when we consider that the Allied nations have come to the United States for the purpose of obtaining arms. As we have a factory in Canada making our own rifles, I think it

is time that this captious criticism with regard to the Ross rifle should come to an end. It has come from hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House and from newspapers throughout *the country. Formerly hon. gentlemen on the other side had the exclusive right to the criticism of the Ross rifle, but the criticism has probably come* from all quarters regardless of politics. One thing I think we all agree about is that we have in Canada a rifle factory where we manufacture an arm which is all right, which enables our people to go out and take part in this conflict and which in time of waT it is important we should have in Canada. So far as the equipping of troops is concerned, I do not know where we should have been if it had not been for the fact that we had the Ross rifle factory. I am quite sure that we should not have been able to equip 50,000 men, much less 300,0000, if we had been dependent on outside rifle supply. The demand has been so great, not only in the Mother Country, but in everyone of the Allied nations,that if we had not had this factory we should have been absolutely unable to equip any considerable number of men in Canada since the outbreak of war. Reasonable criticism was necessary and desirable, but I think that we should agree now to give up all further discussion of the matter. The problem of [DOT] maintaining forces at home is a very serious one, and I apprehend the difficulties suggested by the Prime Minister as existing in this regard while we are engaged in preparing and sending over as fast as possible these men for overseas service.

In the course of a few months there will be in the province of Nova Scotia a provincial election. The term of the present legislature will expire shortly. There are, I am sure, over 5,000 soldiers under enlistment scattered throughout the province of Nova Scotia at the present moment. It is rumoured that all the regiments now recruited and recruiting will be sent to Aldershot for training during the summer months and until they go to the front. The question therefore naturally arises as to whether any provision can be made in a fair manner for the voting of these citizen soldiers at the forthcoming election in the province.
It does not interest one party more than another, so I should think that both parties would desire to devise some means whereby such of the enlisted men as have votes might have the opportunity of voting. It is possible to arrange this in a small prov-

ince like Nova Scotia. Has the Prime Minister, who is now Acting Minister of Militia, considered this matter, and can he work out some plan whereby these soldiers may have the privilege of casting their votes at the impending election? I do not know that this burden should be cast upon him, but probably the gentlemen representing both political parties from Nova Scotia might get together and appear before him and jointly work out some plan. There are two methods by which the soldiers might ibe enabled to vote, one by giving leave for one or more days to the men in the training camps, so that they might go to their homes and vote. That could only be done with the permission of the Department of Militia, and, of course, if this permission were granted it would have to be granted without discrimination. The other plan would be for the Provincial Legislature to provide for a system of registration and voting prior to the polling day of the election, after the manner of the Act passed by this Parliament the session before last. Of course, such action by the Legislature of Nova Scotia would not be effective without the hearty co-operation of the Department of Militia.
What about those who have gone overseas?
I would eliminate them altogether. My suggestion is that we should make provision only for those who are within the province.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Of course, I would not undertake to propose any method of voting. But it is perfectly obvious that the fact that a man has enlisted for the purpose of defending and fighting for the interests of the Dominion, of the whole Empire, and indeed of the world, ought not to be allowed to debar him from exercising his franchise. The fact that he has enlisted is an additional reason why he should have the opportunity of polling his vote, if it is possible to do so by any reasonable means. I understand that the subject is under consideration in the Legislature of Nova Scotia, and that a committee of that Legislature to-day considered two proposals.

I do not think
that is correct.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I may be misinformed. All I can say at the moment is that, so far as we can co-operate in any
reasonable way to assist in arriving at some arrangement to enable the soldiers to poll their votes, we shall be prepared to do so. If the Legislature of Nova Scotia is formulating any method it would be inadvisable for us to take any action until that method has been placed before us in the regular way.
What does the Prime Minister think of the idea of giving a sufficient leave to the enrolled men to permit them to vote?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would be inadvisable for me to express any opinion with regard to that without first consulting the Chief of the General Staff, the Adjutant General, and the other officers of the department, who would know much better than I would whether or not that would be feasible. I shall be very glad to place the observations of my hon. friend before them and ask them for a report on the subject. I do not know whether the proposals which I understood were under consideration would involve any 'question as to the men from the province w^io are* already overseas. Some of them are in Great Britain and some, doubtless, in France. In some of the provinces where provincial elections are impending arrangements have been proposed by which men who have already gone overseas might be enabled to vote. However, my hon. friend has not raised that.
I think it would be inadvisable to do that.

It seems to me that the only feasible plan in connection with provincial elections would be the granting of sufficient leave for those Vho wished to vote to get away and cast their votes, providing everybody gets leave. AM the soldiers would not want to go home to cast their votes. We all know that in any election 25 per cent of those on the voters' list do not come out and take advantage of their franchise. Among the soldiers many, if they were at home, would not vote, and while we should all like to see all the soldiers vote who wished to_vote, it seems to me that for a province to adopt the very unreasonable legislation that we adopted for soldiers to vote abroad, would be a mistake. I think they ought to be given leave so that they may go and vote if they so desire.

Might I ask the Prime Minister if to-morrow afternoon he will put himself in a position to say whether or not it would be possible, in the judgment of the officers of the department.

to grant leave to enable soldiers to vote, so that it would be known? The Legislature of Nova Scotia will not be in session very long, and if anything is to be done in the way of legislation it will have to be done very promptly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Legislation here?
Yes, or there. There will not likely be any necessity for legislation here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I should not think that legislation will be necessaiy here. It would seem to be a question for the Legislature of Nova Scotia to take into consideration in the first instance. I am afraid that I shall have a pretty busy morning before me.
- Mr. MACLEAN: Monday?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I shall make an effort to get the information at the earliest possible moment.

There are two ways in which the votes of soldiers in Nova Scotia, a comparatively small province, and accessible for voting purposes at all points, might be polled, and that would be either by allowing the men to go home, or by enabling the men to cast their votes while in camp. One can see a great many difficulties that would attach to three or four battalions, representative of the whole province and many different counties, casting their ballots in camp. The difficulty of working that out on election day would tax the patience and ingenuity of the' officers in charge. I assume that in regard to this question any attitude that would be adopted by the federal authorities who have control over these men, would not be in any way partisan or inconsistent with the idea that it would be important if possible for these men to exercise the franchise. I understand that in the western provinces a large number of men have been permitted to go and work at the crops.	There is no reason why leave
should not	be given	to	those
who desire to go and cast their votes. Of course, a large number of young men whose names are not on the list, and men whose names are not on the list for some other reason would not need to go home. But those who have votes and who desire to go should be given that opportunity. It would only mean three days' leave, and being in camp it is not as if they were located in a desultory way throughout the country. All the ordinary
	,
details of the camp would be carried on in their absence. I do not profess to be a military expert, but I have been in camps several times, and for a matter of three days the disjointing of things would not be serious because there would be enough men left for ordinary purposes. It seems to me that in bur province that would be the imost feasible method of working it out.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Give them leave?
Give them leave.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And provide transportation ?
Yes, if that is thought desirable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Would not we be subject to the penalties of the Election Act?

I do not think that my hon. friend need have any fear on that score. I am sure that the Prime Minister approves of the desire of the men to have the opportunity of casting their votes, and I also feel confident that a scheme can be worked out with the least inconvenience to the men and the least difficulty to all concerned.- It is impossible to tell anything of the political complexion of the men who are there, but it would be an anomaly if the 3,000 or 4,000 men who are in camp should not be permitted to go home for the -purpose of casting their votes. I hope the Prime Minister will be able to work it out.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Of course, any question as to the political opinions of the men would not be taken into account at all. The only object to be arrived at would be to give the utmost possible freedom to exercise their franchise without any undue influence of any kind, and to provide every facility for that purpose so far as reasonably consistent with military considerations.
Mr. TURRIFF The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) rather gave the idea that we on this side of the House were unduly criticising, and not giving credit to, the Government for the manner in which the raising of the army had been carried out. I do not think anybody on this side of the House has any such idea in his mind. But I do not see that there is any such fulsome praise due to the Government, or the department, in connection with the sending across of an army to the Old Country. You only have to look to Australia with half of our popula-

tion and half our resources to see what she has done; Australia has sent more men to the front than we have. I would like to ask if there is any rule or system under which men are sent forward. I know of regiments that have been kept 18 months in Canada while other regiments that have not been in training half as long have been sent to the front.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What regiment has been here for 18 months?
There was a regiment in Regina. It may have been one of the regiments that passed through here the other day, but they started organizing 17 or 18 months .ago.
Have there been no drafts from any of these regiments? In some cases there have been drafts of 150 or 200 men.

In some cases perhaps
drafts have gone over but in other cases there have been regiments ready for over a year and they do not seem to be chosen to go while other regiments which have not been organized nearly as long have been sent to the front. Is there any rule or system under which the different regiments are sent over.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am informed
by the deputy minister that there was greater delay than usual in the case of some mounted regiments organized in the West. There was no occasion for the use of mounted men on account of the kind of warfare that has been carried on during the past year or fifteen months. After a good deal of correspondence an arrangement was reached by which they could be sent forward as infantry; but for that purpose, I understand, it was necessary that they should go through a different kind of training. Further than that, the deputy minister informs me that a regiment at Regina, which is possibly the one that the hon. gentleman has in mind, has sent forward drafts of about 500 men. When these drafts were sent forward, it was necessary to enlist new men and train them, and a good deal of time was occupied in that way. However, the regiment is about to go forward, as I understand.
One went forward last week from here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It has either
gone forward or is about to go forward.
In the end it will go forward as one of the finest regiments in all the Canadian Expeditionary Forces.

Following the remarks of my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), I appreciate quite as much as he does the very great burden that is carried by the Prime Minister, especially since he has assumed the duties of Acting Minister of Militia, and I certainly would not wish to add to hie burden in any way. But we are here in a very responsible position, dealing with a matter that is of greater and graver import than any that has yet come before any iParliament of the Dominion of Canada, and I consider that we should be doing very much less than our duty if we did not bring into this council of Parliament the best we have, both as to constructive and, if you like, destructive criticism. We wish to secure the highest degree of efficiency in the military administration and service of this Dominion, both for our credit and for the welfare of the Empire, and I hope that neither the Prime Minister nor any other member of the Government will think that in anything said by myself or any other member on this .side of the House we have any other desire than to secure the best that can be had in the interests of the country and of the Empire. We must necessarily criticise from time to time; and in opposition to the very broad statement of commendation that my hon. friend has made, I would be compelled to make an equally broad statement of condemnation, based upon the information that has been given to the House by the Prime Minister to-night, as to the condition of the country in the matter of rifle armament.
We have been in a condition of war ever since August, 1914. When war was declared we were -supposed to have armament for a force, I think, of some 75,000 or 100,000 men. We had a contract, I believe, with a rifle factory in Canada for the purpose of providing a sufficient output to equip our forces. Now, if it is a fact that at the end of eighteen months or more of war we are not in a position to equip efficiently even the forces we have sent overseas-and we have not sent our forces overseas nearly as rapidly as the understanding on which the men were enlisted would require-I cannot' find in that condition of affairs anything for commendation of the Government, either of its activity or of its success. I am not prepared to urge culpabil-

ity against the Government for not having met the exigency more fully.
Would the hon. gentleman suggest where and from whom the Government can secure rifles?

That is not a fair question addressed to a private member. The Government of the country is responsible for the direction of its affairs; it is upon the shoulders of the Government that that responsibility rests, and it is not for any private membeT of Parliament to be held responsible for the direction of the country's affairs. When we faced the condition of war that we did face in the summer of 1914 we must have contemplated at that time an enormous increase in our military forces and equipment, and we surely should have taken stock then with a view to meeting the requirements as they arose.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: At what date?
At the beginning of the war.
No one dreamed of the developments that have arisen.

I am at a loss to conceive how any person could think this war was going to be any other than it has been. With all Europe under arms, with millions of men on both sides ready to take the field, with the training and preparation of two generations, I am at a loss to conceive how anybody could expect that this war would end in a very short time, or would not become the most tremendous conflagration the world had ever seen. My hon. friend has asked what my suggestion is. My suggestion is that the Government was remiss in not making preparation for equipping our forces on a larger scale
10 p.m. than they did. We have a rifle factory in Quebec. I know of no reason why we should not have had a rifle factory in Toronto and another in Montreal. WTe have established shell factories all over Canada; we have established fuse factories in different parts of Canada; and I know of no reason why we should not have increased our output of rifles to any amount that was desired, in the interval that has taken place since the beginning of the war. There may be reasons that I am not aware of that limit the action of the Government, but that is my answer to my hon. friend's question.

It is a very poor one.
	.

I think it is an absolute answer. The weapon that wins the war is the rifle; efficiency in the use of that weapon is the chief factor in winning the war. Any country that presumes to accept a condition of warfare, and does not make adequate preparation for equipping its troops with rifles, and give them an opportunity for acquiring efficiency in the use of that weapon, is not considering the matter seriously.
Does the hon. gentleman claim that the Government was remiss in not supplying these rifles previous to 1914? Or is he referring to the interval since that date?

Since that date. Remiss
in not recognizing that a state of war had occurred in which it might be expected that Canada would have to put forth her military strength to a degree that was never contemplated in time of peace; remiss in not recognizing that the exercise of that strength would necessarily involve the equipping of an enormous number of men with efficient rifles, above everything else. Yet under those conditions of world war, we depended upon exactly the same institution as supplied us with rifles, possibly a sufficient number, in times of peace. That was not a reasonable proposition on the face of it, and it has not worked out well.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What does the hon. gentleman say we should have done?

I have already said that
the Government when it saw the condition of war that had occurred, and it was quite evident that Canada would require to put forth military strength far beyond what she had ever dreamed of in times of peace, was remiss in continuing to depend upon the same mechanical organization- the factory at Quebec-to supply the needs of the country in time of war that had been adequate to supply its needs in time of peace.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Who told the
hon. gentleman that we had to depend upon the same organization?

I understand that we had only one factory when the war began and that we have only one factory yet. We could have multiplied our means for the manufacture of rifles just as we have multiplied our means for the manufacture of shells, fuses, or any other article that was required for military purposes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
It does not matter what occurred before July, 1914; what we are interested in is what is occurring now and what will occur in the immediate future. What the Prime Minister has said as to the increase in the output of rifles is very good so far as it goes; the only trouble is that it does not go far enough. If it was possible to increase the output of rifles fifteen-fold, it was just as possible to increase that output twenty-fold, that is to say, to have secured sufficient rifles to arm and equip our soldiers as they ehould be armed and equipped under the conditions as we find them to-day. Let me remind the House that exactly the same sort of talk was put up in the United Kingdom in the winter of 1914-15 as to the supply of munitions there for use in the war. The people of Great Britain and the Empire were told that everything was being done that could be done; but it turned out that everything that could be done was not being done, and under the stress of criticism, exertions were put forward that had not been put forward before, and the supply of munitions was increased and still increased until we believe that today they have an adequate supply. If, however, the Government and the people of the United Kingdom had rested, in tlje winter of 1914-15 as easily as this Government are resting now in regard

to the supply of rifles for the soldiers of Canada, the war would never have been won by the Allies; it would have been lost. This is no time for recrimination; it is no time for blaming this one or that one or the other one; this is the time to recognize the conditions that we have to face and to meet those conditions adequately, and the first thing we need in order to take our proper part in this war is a sufficient supply of efficient rifles in the hands of proficient men. Unless and until we have that, we are not taking that part that we all desire to take in the task of winning this war. I did not know the condition was as the Prime Minister has said it is; I regret that it has had to be stated that we are short of rifles; but I would be doing far less than my duty as a member of this House if I did not use this opportunity of impressing, so far as I can impress, upon the Government, the House and the country, the fact that we must have an adequate supply of efficient rifles, or else we are not doing our part in the winning of the war.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would not like my hon. friend to imagine that anything he says impresses that consideration upon the mind of the Government any more than it has been impressed ever since the outbreak of the war., I cannot make that too plain to him. There is nothing that he has said here to-night that we do not know. There is no admonition that he has addressed to us that we did not have in mind fifteen months ago, and, if it had been otherwise, we would not have been able to produce in Canada today an output of rifles fifteen times as great as the output immediately before the war. If we had not takeq that precaution the conditions would not have been as satisfactory as they are to-day. For I consider it a remarkable thing that, in the stress of this war and under the difficulties experienced in getting the complicated machines, too numerous for me to name, which are necessary for the purpose of establishing now units in a rifle factory, and with the growing demand all over the United States for that machinery on account of the orders for rifles that were coming from all the Allies to the United States-I say, I consider the results obtained in Canada are wonderful results. Not only had the machines to be provided, but it was necessary to procure all the material, material of a very precise type and difficult to procure-the seasoned wood, the special descrip-

tion of steel, and all the articles which go into these rifles. These articles had to be procured in quantities fifteen or twenty times as great as any provision had been made for before the war. And, as I have said, all this had to be done in competition with the great industrial concerns in the United States that had orders for millions of rifles from all the governments in Europe. The matter for astonishment is not that more was not done, but that so much was done, and that Canada, up to the present time, has been substantially able to arm every soldier with an efficient rifle before he crossed the Atlantic, the , exceptions being, as I am informed by the deputy minister, two or three regiments whose rifles were not taken with them,	but
followed them very shortly afterwards. I repudiate any suggestion of remissmess on the part of the Government, and I say that the results that have been obtained are a credit to Canada.

This is the most important question connected with the war and with Canada's participation in that war, and the Prime Minister will pardon me if I pursue the argument a little further. I have discussed the question of the supply of rifles for the active militia and for what may be called the auxiliary militia, the home guard. We are now aware that the reason these people are not equipped with weapons is that it was not possible to supply them. But we are assured that our troops as they go overseas are supplied with efficient rifles, and the Prime Minister tells us in detail of the difficulties of supplying rifles more rapidly than they have been supplied. I quite appreciate that there are difficulties. But let me turn the other side of the question. We are sending men overseas-our men- to meet on the field of battle the most highly-trained and best equipped troops the world ever saw. We are not doing justice to our troops unless, when we send them into the field, they have the best equipment that we can furnish them and unless they are as efficient and as proficient in the handling of that equipment as it is possible for them to be. Now I am to be corrected here and now if what I state is not right. According to the best information I have, our troops, enlisted in Canada and kept in training in Canada for periods of from six months to fifteen months, have gone over to England or the Continent, as the case may be, without

ever having had efficient target practice. Not to speak too generally, my information is that at the Sarcee camp near Calgary last summer there were 8,000 men in brigade camp, and that these 8,000 men had something over sixty-odd service rifles with whioh to carry on target practice. The only target practice they received was with these sixty-odd rifles for a period of four or five months in the summer camp. I saw some of these regiments going through here the other day. And I say that if the facts are as I have stated them-and I am here to be corrected if they are not-this country did not do its duty-
Are you sure of the facts?

I am, but if I am wrong let me be corrected now. These men have gone to face the enemy on the battlefields of Europe, and, according to my information, they have not had fair opportunity to become proficient in the use of that weapon which is the decisive factor in modern battle, either in attack or defence. The Deputy Minister of Militia is at the elbow of the Prime Minister, and he can say whether that is right or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
And he says
absolutely it is not right. I will tell the hon. gentleman why it is not right. In the first place, so far as regiments in Canada are concerned, the best provision of rifle available has been given to them for target practice, not usually Mark III Ross rifle, but Mark II Ross rifle when the other was not available. I do not say they have always had the full equipment for a battalion, but I am assured by the deputy minister that they have had a sufficient number of rifles to enable target practice to be carried on efficiently at every camp. But my hon. friend goes further and says that they have not only gone overseas to Great Britain without instruction but they have gone from Great Britain to France without instruction.
So far as we know.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
But the hon. gentleman should not without warrant make statements which disquiet public opinion in this country and which are without foundation. I say that when these men go overseas they go through a course of musketry instruction at one of the English schools. I mv&elf, when in England last summer, saw regiment after regiment going out for instruction at the
great musketry school at Hythe. I say from my knowledge,-and I think I know as much of this matter as does the hon. gentleman-that not one regiment from Canada has gone to the war without adequate instruction in musketry. If they have not got it on this side they have got it on the other side. And I deprecate strongly statements of that kind which will appear in the public press of Canada and which tend to disquiet the parents, relatives and iriends of those who have gone overseas to fight for their country.

Perhaps a person who has been there and seen can speak with knowledge. The question has been raised as to the training of these men in the use of the rifle. A number of. years ago the British Army changed its method of training. The men are now trained with dummy ammunition; they are not allowed to go on the rifle range and fire live ammunition until they have obtained a considerable degree of efficiency with dummy ammunition. The idea is that instead of going in for this long range target practice the men must he able to put twenty-five or thirty shots a minute in an 18- inch ring at 400 yards. The men are practised constantly in this aiming and rapid firing with dummy ammunition. Even at the front every man is on his honour bound to devote a certain amount of time to this practice, and each day he goes through these motions for at least ten minutes in order to acquire proficiency in rapid aiming and firing. I was at Sarcee Camp, and I know that the training there was of that kind. When the training is of that kind it is not necessary to have a great number of rifles; a few rifles will suffice. A man who fires five rounds on the rifle range after he has completed his practice in this way, is far more efficient than if he had been working for two or three weeks under the old system and costing the Government a large sum of money for cartridges. Soldiers of the old school 'appreciate the fact that the men are not firing away hundreds of dollars worth of ammunition at the targets every day. I know that the units that have gone to England get thorough training in this modern school of musketry, which, after all, is the school that stood the British Army in such good stead in the retreat from Mons, and that has made the Canadians such an efficient fighting force at the front. When I left England last summer, the number of men without rifles in tho new army regiments,



when I saw them on the march, was far greater than the number without them in Sarcee camp. They had not made any provision for the war, but they were making rifles as fast as they could. The units that went to the Dardanelles got their rifles at Malta; these rifles were sent over from India for them.
The great dearth of rifles has been one of the drawbacks of this war. I suppose that possibly one-third of Kitchener's army is not yet supplied with rifles in England. Fully one-half of the men were drilling in civilian clothes and had been doing so all winter-or in old uniforms of the blue and red type which is now obsolete. I think, therefore, that we have made fairly good progress in this respect. When I came over and found the regiments all equipped with uniforms I was very much surprised, because in England fully threetquarters of the men did not have uniforms. As to the rifle practice, if the men are given rifle practice according to the new school, they do not need any rifle at all except a rifle in form that has two sights on it. It is like the old deer shooting idea, that men mu6t be' able to raise a rifle rapidly and drop the enemy. Some of the English soldiers who are very proficient fire as many as thirty-five rounds a minute. In that kind of training it is not necessary to spend thousands of dollars on the ranges. They were indulging in the new practice at Sarcee when I inspected them last fall, and they had made fair progress in it, and were doing very well. They did not have rifles for every one there, but I do not think that is necessary; if the men get new Tifles after they are trained and go to the field, it is possibly the best way. I think we are doing very well so far as that is concerned. Of course, not 5 per cent of the people of Great Britain or the colonies and dependencies believed what Lord Kitchener said when the war broke out, that it would last two and possibly three years. The men who could get articles in the magazines and those who could hold put lie meetings and be listened to were the ones who would tell the whole world that the war was going to end in two months; that Germany would be starved by that time. In some places the same idea still prevails, but I do not think many members of this House, if I asked them when the war was going to end, would say that it will be over in two or three months. I stated in the House once before this session [Mr. Currie \
that the war would last more than another year, and in that I was very seriously brought to task by some of my associates, in the House and outside, who said that I was dreaming; that the war would be over in two or three months. I fail to see that. I think we are on the crest of the war at the present time; the situation at Verdun to-day shows the first sign that the Allies are going to win. If they make the best of progress it will take them another year or year and a half-but there is no doubt as to what the end will be.

There was a question of fact as between the Premier and myself in regard to the armament of the men at the Sarcee camp at Calgary. What the hon. member for North Simcoe has said substantiates my statement that the men at the Sarcee camp were not armed with the Mark III rifle; that they did not have adequate target practice with the 'Mark III rifle.
Sir ROBERT BORDEN I did not say that they were armed with the Mark III rifle.
I made an assertion as to the equipment of the troops there, and I understood the Prime Minister to say that I did not know what I was talking about.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend said that members of the Canadian Expeditionary Forces who went to the front to fight in the trenches had not adequate musketry training. I said that this, according to the information given to me by the deputy minister, was absolutely incorrect, and according to the information it is absolutely incorrect.
Is that as to musketry training in England, or as to musketry training in Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In Canada and in Great Britain. It does not make any difference where they get it as long as they get it before they reach the front.
I was stating a condition as I believe it exists in Canada, and I want to know whether I stated what is correct or not.

The hon. gentleman has
perhaps misconstrued what I said. For instance one company in each battalion would be armed with rifles, either Mark II or Mark III. That is the condition that obtained all over the country. The time table of training is divided up into various things -squad drill, company drill, physical train-

ing, marching; one company would be constantly exercised in the use of arms and arm drill and musketry, whilst others would he employed in something else. I think it would be impossible for the United States, for instance, with all its power, to,, arm the soldiers of Canada in as short a time as would be required to arm them all as they are enlisted.

The question is not as to what could or could not be done; the question is what was done. I repeat that what . I said has been established, that the Canadian troops did not get adequate target practice with the service rifle in Canada, that they were not supplied with service rifles with which they could engage in target practice, and that they went from Canada without having had sufficient or efficient target practice. The hon. member for North Simcoe says that they have some system for practice with dummy ammunition that is better than the practice with the efficient rifle. That may be; I do not know whether that is true or not, but my information is that in order that a man may be efficient in the use of the rifle, he must know the rifle. He must have had the opportunity of practicing with his own. rifle, so that he understands whatever peculiarity there may be in the rifle, or else he will not be efficient. It is said that the only use of rifle shooting in the field is at short range and quickfiring; but I will draw the attention of the House to this fact, that our casualty lists show a larger proportion of injuries from snipers than they do from any other cause except when an occasional great battle occurs.

There are more German
casualties from the sniping of our fellows.

I certainly hope so, but
the point is that the man that can hit the mark at long range is on the showing of the facts the most useful member of the military force, both for offence and defence, and he cannot get that expert ability except by actual practice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would like to tell my hon. friend that I had the authority of the General Officer Commanding the Canadian Expeditionary Force at the front for the statement that the Canadian divisions at the front have been more successful in keeping down snipers, and more efficient in the use of rifles in the respect that my hon. friend alluded to, than any other
222*
part of the British forces that he was aware of.

I am very glad to hear
that, but again I must insist that they are not given all the opportunities that should be given them under the circumstances surrounding their training at the hands of the Militia Department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I may say fur-there that I have had a letter from General Williams within the past two weeks, since our troops have been moved from one portion of the fine that they formerly held to take up another portion of the line, and I have his statement that they were moved there because of their efficiency in that way, and that since they have arrived there they have been most successful in accomplishing the purpose for which they were sent.

We are very glad to know that they have acquired efficiency; but our business was to send them over efficient, and we did not do it because we did not supply them with the rifles that would enable them to become efficient on their home training grounds.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: All I have to say is that General Alderson's and General Williams' statements are absolutely inconsistent with that which my hon. friend has just made.

After this little tussle between my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) and the right hon. Acting Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Robert Borden) I think perhaps we ought to go on in a little different strain. I endorse the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), that under certain circumstances it is very advisable to recall efficient non-commissioned officers, give them commissions and employ them in this country in the training of men who have joined the ranks in the battalions which are now being recruited. I think that is a wise proposition. Young men have been advanced within their own ranks. I know some that have been advanced, but they have not been given commissions. Perhaps it would not be out of place for me to say here that I congratulate the Government on the good work they have done in this dreadful struggle. Not only do I congratulate the Government, but I congratulate the whole citizenship of Canada on coming to the rescue as well as they have done. I was very much pleased when the Prime Minister intimated that

his goal was that we should have 500,000 men from Canada on the fighting line. I was glad to hear him announce that there had been recruited from the first of January until the 15th April about 101,000 men-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, nearly 103,-
000.
I was glad to hear that. You may consider me rather pessimistic, but I regret that recruiting has not been so active since that time.
Why?

If there is anything the Government can do to make it more active it behooves them to do it, and I am sure that in that they will have the hearty support of the people of Canada as a whole. I think I should also congratulate the Government upon the splendid help of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, who has come so boldly to the front and given his heartfelt support to the Government on this occasion.
And his followers?

His followers too. It was my privilege to state in this House, during a session before this, that the Government must expect criticism in connection with their administration and the expenditure of the moneys entrusted to them; but that does not mean that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House do not support them in their undertaking in defence of home and country, and of this great Empire. The Acting Minister of Militia said to my hon. friend from Edmonton that he would like him to make a prophecy as to the extent of the war. Let me just read one line from a letter I received this morning from the front, almost from the trenches, from a soldier who was wounded last October, but who is now back fighting as a private in the First Brigade Machine Gun Company, First Canadian Division.
Would my hon. friend give us the name of that soldier?

This is a matter that is
private. I could give it to my hon. friend if he wants to know, but it would be considered rather personal if I were to name him. But what is in the letter is this: " I do not see how anything but the wastage of men will end the war." That does not indicate that the end of the war is near at hand. It means that it will not end in the near future, and it devolves upon us to find a way of reaching the goal that the

Prime Minister mentioned, and that is that before the New Year we should have the full total of half a million men enrolled from Canada. I do not know how this is to be overtaken, but as one member of the House I should be very glad to give every support to the Government who have this great undertaking in hand. It isi I am sure, an undertaking whose extent we did not realize even when the war was declared. There is much to be said in support of the contention of my hon. friend from Edmonton, that there was every indication that the struggle would be a long one, and certainly the indications at the present time are that the struggle will not end in the near future, and it behooves us as a people to do everything in our power to reach the goal that the Prime Minister intimated, at the opening of this new year, it was his desire to reach. I congratulate the Government and the people of Canada, and I congratulate the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who has given such splendid aid and support to the Government in their war measures.	.

Would the
Prime Minister be good enough to tell us what position General Alderson occupies in regard to Canadian troops? It was stated in the press lately that he had ceased to occupy the position of command and that a Canadian had been appointed in his place.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have no official information on the subject.

Now that we have decided that we do not need rifles for target practice, I think we might take up the question of the efficiency of the rifle that we use, that is the Mark III Ross rifle. I have heard some reports with regard to this rifle that have been cited by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, and I would submit that, as the efficiency of this rifle is under suspicion at any rate, there might very well be a careful inquiry as to what its efficiency really is. The matter is too important to be passed over. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister resents the idea of these questions being discussed in this House of Parliament. We in this House of Parliament are charged with the responsibility, on behalf of the people of this country, of seeing that the best is done that can be done, and we are not relieved from that responsibility because of the gravity of the question that has to be considered. We have at the front a reporter, or a person who sends'

reports of what occurs there. His reports, I understand, are supposed to be official. They are given in the newspapers under the heading: " The eyewitness reports " thus and so. I have here two reports of the eyewitness as to the recent fighting in the trenches in France or Flanders, and there are certain statements in these reports which I will take the responsibility of reading to the House, which I cannot read without grave disquiet. This is one of the eyewitnesses's reports. He speaks of certain events and he says:
An insistent bombardment was continued by the enemy, and Anally, about noon, all his remaining rides being out of commission and his men exhausted, Captain Gwynne decided to retreat.
The eyewitness, reporting on another occasion, says:
Waist-deep in mud, the few survivors of our garrison could offer little resistance. Hardly one of their rifles could be got to Are.
He says again: '
The lieutenant emptied his revolver at the Germans and seized a rifle, only to find that it lammed at the first shot. The rifles of his men, again and again reclaimed from the mud, only fired a shot or two before they also jammed.
These are reports of the fighting that has occurred within the last few days. I say that these words are very disquieting to me. I do not want to emphasize the point too strongly, but I say that, in view of statements such as these appearing in the reports of the eyewitness, coupled with information which I have received from soldiers who have served in the trenches, information that is corroborated by other members of the House, I desire to urge upon the attention of the Government the desirability of making such inquiry as to the efficiency of this rifle with which we have armed our soldiers as shall absolutely settle the question as to whether it is a suitable rifle for active service, or the most suitable rifle we can get for active service. There is no doubt about its qualities as a shooting rifle, but my information is that its mechanism is in some parts so delicate that .it is more apt to get out of order than the Lee-Enfield. That is to say, owing to the difficult conditions of active warfare, where it cannot have that care and attention that it would have in an arsenal or under peace conditions, it is more apt to get out of order than is the Lee-Enfield rifle. If that is a fact, it is an unfortunate fact, and we should take steps to alter that condition. I appreciate the responsibility
of the statement I make, but it is because it is of such tremendous importance that I dare to make it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: An inquiry was made into the Ross rifle last year, and I believe into the Lee-Enfield as well, after the jamming to which I have alluded first occurred. As a consequence of that inquiry, the chamber of the Lee-Enfield, as I am informed, and the chamber of the Ross rifle, were enlarged. I have already given the particulars of those changes. The Ross rifle is not used at the front now except with the enlarged chamber. I suppose it might be taken into consideration in connection with the Ross rifle, if my hon. friend desires to criticise it, that 100,000 of these rifles were ordered by the British Government in the early months of the war, and complaints have been made that they have not been delivered as fast as was expected and desired. I am not aware that there is any rifle in the world that might not jam or refuse to fire after it had been imbedded in mud or had fallen, into deep mud in a trench. I should imagine, although I do not profess to be an expert in rifles, that there is nothing very extraordinary in that, nor do I imagine that the Lee-Enfield or any other rifle would be immune from difliculties of that kind. The Ross rifle may be superior in some respects-I believe it is-to the Lee-Enfield. It is quite possible that in some other respects it may not be as serviceable as that rifle. I am, prepared neither to affirm not to deny as to these matters, because I do not know about them. Very likely if you got a number of experts to give you opinions about both rifles they would not entirely agree among themselves. It is probably true that of any two types of rifle that you select, one would have certain advantages, and the other rifle in comparison with it, certain other advantages. As my hon. ' friend says, the Ross rifle, for accurate long-distance shooting, is perhaps the beet rifle in the world.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It may be equally true that the very qualities which gave it that pronounced advantage may be attended with a certain disadvantage under other conditions; I do not know, but one can readily see that that is possible. I believe it is true that the British soldiers who are very good shots and are employed for the purpose of long-distance shooting -sniping, as it is called-are very apt to

throw away their own rifle when they have a chance to pick up a Boss. -On the other hand, I have heard, as no doubt my hon. friend has, that'some of our own men sometimes throw away the Ross rifle when they *can pick up a Lee-Enfield. An inquiry was made into the Roes rifle last year. The difficulty about the chamber was discovered. The jamming, as I understand it, was not entirely due to the chamber, but, to a certain extent, to the character of *some ammunition that had been issued, and which I think is no longer being issued. With ammunition of a different character, and especially with that produced in Canada, I am informed that even before the chamber was enlarged there was not very much difficulty with jamming so far as the Ross rifle is concerned.

I would suggest that
means be taken, not to hold a formal court, but to have the privates who come back to Canada from the front interviewed, not by an officer, but by some person to whom they would be willing to state the facts as they believed them to be. In that way the Government could satisfy itself as to the rifle. I do not think a Military Board is a good way of getting at what the soldier actually thinks of the rifle. He would not talk as freely when he was in the position of a witness or of a criminal in the dock as he would to some reliable person to whom he could give his opinion casually as to the rifle. In the multitude of expressions of opinion the Government would have a pretty fair basis to go upon as to the worth of the rifle. This is a terribly serious matter.

How could the hon. gentleman depend upon the opinion of the soldier when, as he told us only a moment ago, the soldier does not know anything about the rifle? He was not trained to handle it, and did not even know one end from the other; that was his argument.
Oh, no.

The hon. gentleman said that the soldier had not been properly >
trained in musketry, and did not understand anything about the rifle.
I did not say anything of the kind.

A man who does not know anything about the rifle is not the one whose opinion you should take, especially a man who does not know one

end from the other. 'The hon. gentleman is absolutely inconsistent.

The hon. gentleman has put words into my mouth that I never used, and ideas that I never expressed and have never held. I argued that the soldier had not a fair opportunity of becoming efficient in rifle shooting. I did not argue that he did not have every opportunity of becoming acquainted with the mechanism of the rifle. Surely the man who has been to the front knows what the rifle can do, and I am suggesting that his opinion be taken rather than that of some alleged expert. The man whose life has depended on the rifle is the man whose opinion I am willing to ask and depend upon.

Perhaps the Acting
Minister could give me some information, if not now the next time these Estimates are up, as to rentals of recruiting offices in the city of Ottawa. There are two recruiting offices, one on the corner of Sparks street and Elgin, and the other a little way-down on Elgin street, within a stone's throw of each other. As only a few men join daily at each of these places I think one building would be enough. There is a third building used for the same purpose a little further down Sparks street. I should like to know what rental has been paid since the war started for all recruiting offices. Also how much it has cost the department to guard the canal at Cardinal, Iroquois and Morrisburg since the war started. In my opinion the cost has been unnecessarily heavy.
Would there be any objection to giving information as to the number of machine guns provided for each battalion in the field?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
Do the heavier guns use
heavier ammunition than rifle ammunition?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is all the same ammunition, but the question depends upon the particular purpose for which the gun is used. One type of gun can be taken up and moved very quickly; the other is used in a different way and is usually placed where it will be in a permanent position for a certain period of time.

The Prime Minister, I see, does not desire to say how many guns are supplied to each battalion. I am going to ask the question:	Have the battalions
actually in the field been supplied with the full quota of machine guns, whatever that may be?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The deputy minister informs me, yes, absolutely so.

Have the battalions in
training in Great Britain been supplied with their full quota of machine guns?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They are supplied in Great Britain with a sufficient number for practice. Even if there should be the greatest abundance of machine guns, I am informed that they would not receive more than enough for practice while they are in training. They receive their full quota only when they go to the front.

What is the position of
the battalions organized and in training in Canada in regard to the supply of machine guns?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The arrangement in Canada has been the same, that they are supplied with a sufficient number to enable training to be carried on.

Would the minister be
good enough to say what number of machine guns for training were supplied to the 51st, the 63rd, and the 66th Battalions during the past winter?

I really think the hon.
member should not ask that question, because the number of guns supplied to each army corps could be figured out.
I do not think so. If the hon. gentleman will wait until I get the answer, I think he will find it has no bearing on that matter at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: With regard to the battalions which the hon. gentleman has mentioned, they were all located where machine gun practice could not be carried on during the winter months.

The fact is that the three battalions were in Edmonton last winter, and when I saw them one of them had one machine gun and the other two had none. Therefore the machine gun sections of those battalions did not have a fair opportunity to become proficient in t'he use of the machine gun. Again I take the liberty of saying that I do not think that is a fair position to put our soldiers in.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Where were the battalions stationed?
The 51st Battalion was located in the drill hall, and the 63rd and the 66th were in the exhibition building at Edmonton.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am informed that machine-gun training would not be carried on under those conditions, but that the men, when they go into camp, will receive machine-gun training.

They were at the Sarcee camp last summer, and they did not have machine guns there to train with. The fact that one battalion at Edmonton should have a machine gun and the other two none rather breaks down the idea of maChine-gun practice not being carried on in the winter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Machine guns, like rifles, cannot be procured in a moment. Orders were given immediately after the war broke out, but you do not get delivery of machine guns within a few months after they are ordered, sometimes not for a year. The companies which have been manufacturing machine guns have been making pretty good deliveries. It might possibly be that during the period which my hon. friend mentioned there were not machine guns available.
There are at the present time five battalions being recruited. Some of them are Up to strength and all of them are training. How many of those bat-taliens have machine guns to train with?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I really could
not say at the moment; I will get the information for my hon. friend.

The battalions are the
138th, the 151st, the 202nd-the deputy minister will know the numbers. I just want to emphasize the point that I have urged to-night, that the men are not receiving the opportunity to become proficient that is an absolute necessity for their welfare and for ours.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not agree with that, if my hon. friend speaks of the period at which they go to the front. So far as I am informed, they do receive adequate training in machine gun practice before they go to the front. If they do not receive the whole of it in this country, they receive further training and instruction on the other side before they are sent to the front. I am quite confident that the system of inspection on the other side is sufficiently thorough to ensure efficiency before the men are sent to the trenches.

The 51st Battalion was
recruited at Edmonton beginning in the fall of 1914. It was recruited to full strength some time in January or February of 1915. It went overseas in March of 1915. It was there for over a year, yet all the target practice that the battalion had is what I have stated at the Sarcee camp, and that battalion in the barracks at Edmonton was the fortunate possessor of the one machine gun that was at Edmonton for training purposes. I just wish to ask in regard to machine guns, if the Prime Minister does not object, as to the pattern of the machine gun that is used.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The two classes that are used are the Colt machine gun and the Lewis.

The Lewis machine gun,
as I understand it, is the later and most approved pattern for military use. It is the one that is used, for instance, in aircraft. I would like to ask why the Colt is used instead of the Lewis.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They are used
for different purposes. The one is a heavier gun that the other. I mentioned to my hon. friend a moment ago that we had a communication on the subject requiring a certain proportion of the heavier gun and a certain proportion of the lighter gun. I am not enough of a military expert to set forth an exposition of the particular reasons which have influenced this decision; it is enough for me that the military authorities, who are supposed to be competent, have fixed a certain proportion of each, and, unless we supply our men with that proportion, they will not be allowed to go to the front.

I am not very much of a military man myself, but this question of machine guns is very important, as is also the question of the efficiency of machine guns. My information is that the
rJVlr. Oliver.]
advantage	of	the	Lewis machinegun is	that it is	air-cooled;
the Maxim is water-cooled, and the Colt is not cooled at all. The advantage of the Lewis is that it can be fired continuously without becoming too hot. In the case of the Maxim, rapid firing heats the water and causes steam which exposes the position of the gun. The Lewis can be fired continuously without exposing the position. As the Prime Minister has said, it uses the same ammunition as the Colt, that is, the ordinary rifle ammunition. It is inconceivable to me, when there are two guns using the same ammunition, and one offering a tremendous advantage over the other, why the one having the least advantage is used at all. In the Colt gun, in order to overcome the heating, the gun is provided with one or two extra barrels and when one becomes heated it is unscrewed and taken off and the cool one put in its place, when the gun is ready again to fire. It appears to me that a gun that requires that exchange of barrels is tremendously handicapped in actual use as compared with one like the Lewis that will fire as long as the ammunition lasts. There does not appear to me any good reason for the use of the Colt gun in preference to the Lewis, unless it should be that a sufficient supply of the Lewis gun cannot be secured.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Has the hon.
gentleman any idea of how long it takes to change the barrel in the Colt gun?
It does not take very long, of course, but under battle conditions, the loss even of seconds may make a great difference in the result.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I can console my hon. friend as to the Colt gun in one respect, that is very creditable to the ingenuity of two of our Canadian officers at the front. The Colt gun has three barrels. When one becomes hot it is removed and another put in its place, which, in its turn, is replaced by the third, and by the time that is heated the first barrel is supposed to have cooled sufficiently to be used again. It used to take a minute and ten seconds under the old system, to make the change of barrels, and the change was made without protection to the man who made it. But two of our officers at Shorncliffe invented an improvement, which is very easily made, and with which, by means of what is called an interrupted screw, a principle applied in the big guns, the barrel can be changed in eight or ten seconds, and the man is pro-

tected while making it. After a review at Shomcliffe last year, these two officers asked Sir Archibald Murray, General Hughes and myself to look at the improvement they had made. Sir Archibald Murray, who understands these matters very well,, said that the device was perfectly feasible and a great improvement. The Minister of Militia directed that all the guns should have this improvement made without delay. lit was regarded as rather a quick piece of administration to arrange it in that way. One British officer who was present said it would take weeks, if not months, to accomplish that under the regular system in vogue in military affairs in most countries. The Colt gun is regarded as a suitable gun by the authorities of the War Office. It is used for brigade formation, while the Lewis gun is for company formation. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman has observed the regiments that have passed through Ottawa. Recently I had the privilege of seeing one every day for six days. Each of these regiments has a machine gun section, made up, as I recollect it, of some sixteen to twenty-four men, who are thoroughly trained in the use of the gun. Besides, there is the brigade formation which ie supplied, in respect of each brigade, with the Colt gun, a heavier gun than the other and used for more permanent positions. Whether that is right or wrong from a military standpoint I am not ,in a position to judge, but I do feel that I at least am not in a position to overrule the authorities of the War Office on that subject.

I desire to ask the Prime Minister with regard to a case I mentioned the other night, of Private Chapman of the 106th Battalion, at Trenton, Nova Scotia. I received a letter from a sergeant, wounded and invalided home, who said that the treatment accorded this man was very bad. Perhaps the right hon. gentleman, if he has the papers, will show them to me.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) made some inquiry into a similar case. He asked me to postpone the discussion of it until he was here. There is no reason, however, why I should not give certain information in the meantime. The memorandum handed to me is as follows:
As I have already informed you, the Adjutant General has given direct instructions to stop this kind of punishment. Although there is nothing in our Canadian regulations dealing
with the subject matter, the British regulations entitled " Manual of Military Law " page 721, deals with field punishment. Sub paragraph (d) of paragraph (a) reads: "When in irons a soldier may be attached for a period or periods not exceeding two hours of any one day to a fixed object, but he must not be so attached during more than three of any four consecutive days, nor during more than twenty-one days in all." Our officers commanding have applied this regulation notwithstanding the fact that it is no more applied in the British army. They have done it through ignorance and over zeal. The Adjutant General has given instructions that all kinds of field punishment, excepting detention, are not to be applied for the future. Therefore, I hope there will be no further recurrence of such cases.
There is in the memorandum some information with regard to particular cases, showing that there was very great insubordination. There are also reports of the medical officers which show that there was no physical injury.

Would the Prime
Minister place the papers on the Table so that I may look at them?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will do so. I agree entirely with the view expressed that punishment of that kind, which is not only unusual but might be regarded as cruel, should not be applied in our expeditionary force. I am sure the Ajutant General will see to it, as he has promised, that nothing of that kind shall occur -in the future.
I think that some attention should be paid to the officers who undertake to apply that kind of punishment.

As an officer I deprecate very much the discussion of matters of this kind in the House. It is subversive to discipline. In England, according to the King's regulations, there are two kinds of field punishment: Field punishment No. 1 and field punishment No. 2. Field punishment No. 1 is the form of punishment that has been administered to this man.
