When a soldier is insubordinate at the front he can be tied up; that is the practice in all wars; it was the practice in South Africa. In England they have withdrawn field punishment No. 1, because they have there what they call detention prisons, like that at Gosport. When a man is insubordinate they send him to ' Cosport for a period where he is put through a course of sprouts. When he goes back to his regiment he is very much subdued and a very good soldier. We have no detention prisons in Canada. Although 99 per cent of the men that come

into our regiments are the very best in the world, sometimes magistrates or friends of criminals get them released from prison and they enter our army.
Not in Canada?

Yes. Very often after a man has been before a commanding officer a number of times, having been in the habit of fiercely attacking his comrades, disobeying regulations and acting like a wild beast, it is discovered, perhaps, that he has parole papers in his possession, that he has been a very vicious criminal and that his record here or in the United States is such that they do not want him in the country. The fact that only two cases of the kind referred to have been mentioned as occurring in Canada, speaks very well of the Canadian officers and the discipline that they are enforcing, especially when you consider the number of soldiers who are in training. Evidently there is the feeling that any one of them can write to a member and claim that he was vilely used, and that sort of thing. I feel satisfied that if the facts in this case were gone into it would be found that the men got a great deal less than they would have got in a civil court, and for that Teason I think that possibly the less said about those things the better. It is not so very many years since they used to have flogging in the Army. If it is at all possible to get along with a man without punishing him, I do not think that a single officer in the Canadian Militia would tie him up, but if he gets abusive and threatens to 'kill his comrades, being in a state of madness, perhaps, from drink, you must do something with him. You must tie him up in some way, and you are only allowed to tie him up to a fixed object. I have seen men break through irons four or five times in succession. I have seen men so powerfully built that they could break handcuffs as if they were made of paper. You must do something with these men. The General in command has power to deal with all these questions, and if complaint is made to the divisional officer I feel quite satisfied that if the officers have gone beyond their duty they will be cashiered or court-martialled, and there would not be necessity for bringing the matter before the House.

The reason why I brought this matter to the attention of the committee was a desire to prevent injury to recruiting in the locality. The incident
fMr. Currie.]
to which I refer occurred in a company which was guarding one of the munition works, where, rightly or wrongly, the men engaged in the work interfered with what they thought was excessive punishment. The reason why I mention the matter again is because I have received a letter to-day from a sergeant who had been at the front and who, after distinguishing himself there, had returned home and was engaged in work in a munition factory. This man considered the punishment as improper. While there is a good deal in what my hon. friend not captiously take up complaints of privates against their commanding officers, yet says, that members of the House should there is a phase of the question that he forgets, and it is this: nothing will stop recruiting among the men whom you want to get into the forces like a feeling in the community that the treatment of the men has been improper or unduly severe.
Was this man a soldier or a worker in the munition shops?
He was a soldier.

He may have been
smoking or something like that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Has my hon. friend seen the statement which the soldier made?

Yes, I saw that I received that to-day from another source. As I have said, I received also a letter from Sergeant Grant, who has returned

from the front and who is working in the munition works, who complains about the severity of the punishment. I am aware that the claim is that the soldier had a bad record.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It was not with regard to the character of the punishment. According to the Eastern Chronicle, an investigation was held at which the mayor of Trenton was present, as well as the mayor of New Glasgow, and representatives of local newspapers. The report says:
The soldier was questioned regarding the nature of the punishment given him and stood up against the wall showing the way in which he was fastened. He gave the following statement which he signed:
Statement No. 715631, Private W. P. Chapman, Composite Company, 106th Battalion.
I left the barracks at Trenton without leave at 6 a.m. on the 6th April, 1916. I did not return until 10 p.m., 17th April, 1916. At the time I went absent I was under open arrest (not allowed to leave quarters). On the morning of 18th April I came before Captain Williams on these charges:	1. Absent without
leave from 6 a.m., 6th April until 10 p.m. 17th April; 2, breaking barracks while under open arrest. I was awarded twelve days' detention with No. 1 field punishment. At 11 a.m. I started my first hour's field punishment which consisted of having my wrists handcuffed to a plank five feet ten inches from the ground allowing some leeway in which to ease myself. My feet were firm on the ground. I was released in one hour. I received no bodily injury whatever, and, with the exception of the tired feeling in my arms felt none the worse for the punishment. I further state this to be my sixth offence against military discipline since coming to Trenton on the 14, 15th March, 1916. The punishment was remitted that afternoon, one hour's punishment being all that I did.

The other day I referred to the fact that there were in Canada officers who were over military age, and who, under no circumstances, would be accepted for service at the front, who did not themselves expect to go, and whom nobody expected to go, and I said that some of such men were members of Parliament. Needless to say, my remarks did not refer in any way to members of Parliament or others who have gone to the front, who were of military age or otherwise qualified to go, or who expected to go. I referred only to the class of men to which I have already alluded, namely, those who did not expect to go and could not, by reason of age or any other cause. The acting minister, in referring to my remarks, said that such men might do useful work in Canada by recruiting or getting battalions together, and using their influence as members or as prominent citizens for military purposes. I think the hon. member for
Renfrew (Mr. Graham) made some remarks of a somewhat similar character. My judgment is that the public man or prominent citizen who declines to do -anything he can do in the way of recruiting or anything else to help the cause unless he is appointed an officer and put on the pay-roll, is not worthy of citizenship in Canada, and I do not think that the taxpayers of this country should be called upon, to provide such men with military pay. I believe that the man who is not willing to make that sacrifice and to do anything .he can along that line is the least qualified man for such purposes, not referring in any way to some men who happen to be members of Parliament and who have the qualifications to be officers. Such men should not be debarred from being officers, and they are entitled to their pay as officers and their indemnity as members. I think that 99 per cent of the people of this country will agree with the view I have expressed.
Militia and Defence-clothing, $800,000.

There are other matters
in connection with the military service that should be discussed possibly at some length. Would the minister object to having some items stand?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If we allowed
one item to stand there would be no objection to discussing any matter relating to the Militia on that one item, as we have been doing all evening. Then, of course, there are supplementaries, The explanation of this item is as follows: It is to provide the Militia, both permanent and non-permanent, with clothing and necessaries. No vote was taken for 1915-16, the current year, and consequently provision for 1916-17 is all the more necessary. The Estimate of the Quartermaster General, which I have under my hand, shows a possible total of over $1,000,000 required, but we are asking for only $800,000. Possibly some of this vote . will be used for the reserve militia, to which my hon. friend from Edmonton has called attention this evening, and whom we would be very glad to furnish with uniforms if it should prove practicable to do so.
When the volunteers are provided with military clothing, what is done with their civilian clothing and their personal effects?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They remain in the ownership and at the disposition of the soidier

Royal Military College, $160,000.
A few days ago I referred to the fact, that the advertisement calling for students for the military college at Kingston was not given to some papers that happened to be Liberal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And some that happened to be Conservative too.

The ^acting minister gave as the reason, that there were some Conservative papers that were not allowed to publish it either. The inference I drew was that because all the Conservative papers did not get this advertisement, no Liberal paper would get it. The only paper in the province of Prince Edward Island that desired to have publication of this notice did not receive -it, while several other papers on the Conservative side did publish it. It would appear to be an application of the party patronage system which the acting minister deprecates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I gave the information as it was given to me, that the number of papers was limited and that several Conservative papers which desired to publish it were refused, and doubtless several Liberal newspapers.

Is the inference I draw
correct, that because the Conservative papers are not publishing it the Liberal papers will not be allowed to publish it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I suppose we can all draw any inference we see fit. My hon. friends' inference is so complex in its character that I hardly grasp it.

I do not think it will
be difficult to grasp.
